title: Springs that keep time: stiffness, bouncing and the favourite beat

summary.text: Hang a bottle on rubber bands and make it bounce. A big bounce takes exactly as long as a small bounce, yet four times the weight makes every bounce twice as slow. Then shake the top end of the bands at just the right beat, and tiny movements of your hand make the bottle swing wildly. You will measure how stiff springs are, time their bounces, find a spring's favourite beat, and learn why a rubber band warms up when you stretch it and why a paper clip tires out.
summary.art: A bottle hanging from a chain of two rubber bands on a stick across two chairs, a hand at the top moving up and down, and a ruler beside the bottle showing a big bounce.

intro.hook: Hang a bottle on a rubber band and pull it down a little. Let go and count ten bounces. Now pull it down much further and count ten bounces again. Which takes longer, the small bounces or the big bounces?
intro.text: Most people guess that the big bounces take longer, because the bottle has further to go. You will find out for yourself. This is a clue to something strange about springs. They keep time. Each spring, with its load, has its own beat, and nothing you do to start it changes that beat. In this unit, you will time bounces, learn what does change the beat, and find out what happens when you push a spring in time with its beat, and out of time with it.
intro.art: Two bottles on rubber bands side by side, one pulled down a little and one pulled down a lot, with a stopwatch between them.

outcomes: I can measure how stiff a spring is, in newtons for each centimetre, and compare springs by their stiffness.
I can explain why two springs side by side are stiffer and two springs in a row are softer.
I can time bounces fairly, by timing ten, repeating and finding the time of one bounce.
I can explain that the bounce time depends on the load and the stiffness, and not on the size of the bounce.
I can predict that four times the load makes the bounce time twice as long.
I can explain resonance: small pushes timed with a spring's own beat build up into a big movement.
I can explain why a stretched rubber band warms up and why a paper clip bent back and forth gets tired and breaks.
I can say where springs keep time in the world: watches, atoms and the Sun.

terms.meaning: How much pull a spring needs for each centimetre it stretches. A stiff spring needs a big pull for a small stretch. Scientists also call it the spring constant.
terms.example: A band that stretches 2 centimetres under a 1 newton pull has a stiffness of 0.5 newtons for each centimetre.
terms.art: Two springs side by side with the same 2 newton pull, one stretched a little and one stretched a lot, with labels stiff and soft.

terms.meaning: How much longer a spring or band gets when you pull it. It is the stretched length minus the relaxed length.
terms.example: A band that is 8 centimetres long relaxed and 11 centimetres long under a load has an extension of 3 centimetres.
terms.art: A band relaxed and the same band stretched with a bracket marking the extra length.

terms.meaning: The weight hung on a spring or band, or any pull put on it.
terms.example: A 500 gram packet hung on a band is a load of about 5 newtons.
terms.art: A packet hanging from a rubber band, with an arrow labelled load.

terms.meaning: A movement that goes back and forth again and again, along the same path.
terms.example: A bottle bouncing up and down on a band, and a child on a swing, are both oscillating.
terms.art: A bottle on a band with arrows up and down and a dotted line for the middle position.

terms.meaning: One complete go of an oscillation, from a starting place, out to one side, back through the middle and to the other side, and back to the start.
terms.example: One bounce down and up, back to where you let go, is one cycle.
terms.art: A bottle in four positions: start, low, middle and back to start, with an arrow joining them in a loop.

terms.meaning: The time for one cycle of the bounce. Scientists call it the period.
terms.example: If ten bounces take 8 seconds, one bounce takes 0.8 seconds.
terms.art: A stopwatch showing 8 seconds beside ten small arrows, each marking one bounce.

terms.meaning: How many cycles happen in one second. It is counted in hertz, written Hz.
terms.example: A bounce time of 0.5 seconds means 2 cycles each second, which is a frequency of 2 hertz.
terms.art: A row of 2 bottle bounces drawn along a one second ruler.

terms.meaning: How far an oscillation goes from the middle, the size of the bounce.
terms.example: If you pull the bottle down 4 centimetres and let go, the amplitude is about 4 centimetres.
terms.art: A bottle bouncing, with a ruler showing the distance from the middle to the lowest point.

terms.meaning: The frequency at which a spring and its load bounce on their own, after a small start. It depends on the stiffness and the load.
terms.example: A bottle on a band might have a natural beat of about 1 bounce each second.
terms.art: A bottle on a band with a clock face showing one bounce each second.

terms.meaning: What happens when you push a spring in time with its natural beat. Each push adds to the last one, so the movement grows big.
terms.example: Pushing a swing at the end of each swing makes it go higher with small pushes.
terms.art: A child on a swing with a parent giving small pushes, and the swing arcs getting bigger in three stages.

terms.meaning: The slow dying away of a bounce, because some of its energy turns into heat and sound.
terms.example: A bottle bouncing on a band bounces smaller and smaller until it hangs still.
terms.art: A wavy line that gets smaller and smaller from left to right.

terms.meaning: The slow wearing out of a material that is bent or stretched again and again, even when each bend is small. Tiny cracks grow until the material breaks.
terms.example: A paper clip bent back and forth ten times snaps in half, though one bend would not break it.
terms.art: A paper clip bent back and forth, with a tiny crack growing at the bend and a break at the end.

terms.meaning: The energy stored in something that has been stretched, squashed or bent and will spring back.
terms.example: A stretched catapult band has elastic energy, which turns into the movement of the stone.
terms.art: A stretched rubber band with sparkles in it, and an arrow showing a paper ball flying away.

terms.meaning: Springs joined end to end, one after the other, so the same pull goes through each. Scientists say they are in series.
terms.example: Two bands linked like a chain are two springs in a row.
terms.art: Two rubber bands linked end to end hanging from a hook with a packet at the bottom.

terms.meaning: Springs placed next to each other, so that they share the pull. Scientists say they are in parallel.
terms.example: Two bands hanging next to each other, both holding one packet, are two springs side by side.
terms.art: Two rubber bands hanging side by side from a hook, both holding one packet.

terms.meaning: The sudden bending or folding of a long thin thing that is pushed from its ends. It stays straight until the push passes a limit, then it folds.
terms.example: A tape measure stands straight when it is pulled out, and then folds suddenly if you press the end.
terms.art: A tape measure pulled out and standing out straight, and another one with a sudden kink.

terms.meaning: A very fine coiled spring in a mechanical watch, which makes a small wheel swing back and forth at a steady beat.
terms.example: A mechanical watch ticks each time its balance spring swings the small wheel once.
terms.art: A cut-away of a watch with a tiny wheel and a fine spiral spring in the middle.

terms.meaning: The pull between two atoms that holds them together. Atoms joined by a bond can vibrate, like two balls joined by a tiny spring.
terms.example: In a water molecule, each hydrogen atom is joined to the oxygen atom by a bond that vibrates.
terms.art: A zoom-in on a water molecule drawn as three balls joined by two tiny springs.

explanations.definition: Stiffness tells you how much pull a spring needs for each centimetre it stretches. A stiff spring needs a big pull for a small stretch. We find it by dividing the pull by the stretch.
explanations.description: Two bands can both be elastic, and still feel very different. One feels soft, and the other feels hard to stretch. To put a number on this, hang a known load on the band and measure how much longer it gets. Suppose a 2 newton load stretches a soft band by 6 centimetres and a stiff band by 2 centimetres. The soft band has a stiffness of 2 divided by 6, which is about 0.33 newtons for each centimetre. The stiff band has a stiffness of 2 divided by 2, which is 1 newton for each centimetre. If you draw a graph of the pull against the stretch, a stiff spring gives a steep line, and a soft spring gives a gentle line. The steepness of the line is the stiffness. Scientists call this number the spring constant. It is only a constant while the spring stays inside its elastic limit. The spring in a pen is stiff, with about 1 to 2 newtons for each centimetre. The springs in a car are very stiff, with hundreds of newtons for each centimetre. A rubber band is soft by comparison.
examples: A pen spring may need 1 to 2 newtons to stretch 1 centimetre. A wide rubber band may need 0.5 newtons for the same stretch.
The springs under a bus seat are stiffer than the springs under a bicycle saddle.
A hair tie is much stiffer than a thin rubber band of the same length.
explanations.art: A graph with stretch in centimetres along the bottom and pull in newtons up the side, with a steep line labelled stiff and a gentle line labelled soft.
explanations.context: In the Stiffness League, you rank things by how hard they are to stretch. This card explains how to turn that into a number.

explanations.concept: Two springs in a row, and two side by side
explanations.definition: Two springs in a row are softer than one, because each spring stretches and the stretches add up. Two springs side by side are stiffer than one, because they share the pull.
explanations.description: Link two identical bands end to end, and hang a 5 newton packet on the bottom. The same 5 newtons goes through both bands, so each band stretches as far as a single band would. The total stretch is double. For the same pull, the stretch doubles, so the pair is half as stiff. Now hang the two bands side by side, both holding the same packet. Each band now carries only half the pull, 2.5 newtons, so each stretches only half as far. The pair is twice as stiff. Take a band of stiffness 0.5 newtons for each centimetre. Alone, it stretches 10 centimetres under 5 newtons. In a row, two bands stretch 20 centimetres. Side by side, they stretch 5 centimetres. A rule hides in this: stiffnesses add when springs sit side by side. Cars use this rule. Each wheel has a spring, and the four springs work side by side to hold up the car. A softer car needs softer springs.
examples: One band stretches 10 centimetres under a packet. Two in a row stretch 20 centimetres. Two side by side stretch 5 centimetres.
A bed has many springs side by side, so it is stiff enough to hold a person.
A very long spring is softer than a short one of the same kind, because it is like many short springs in a row.
explanations.art: Three drawings of the same packet: hanging from one band, from two bands linked in a row, and from two bands side by side, with the stretch drawn as 10, 20 and 5 centimetres.
explanations.context: You may have tried two bands in a row and side by side in Class 3. This card explains why the answers come out the way they do.

explanations.concept: What a bounce is, and how to time it
explanations.definition: A bounce is an oscillation. The spring pulls the load back to the middle, the load's speed carries it past the middle, and the spring pulls it back again. One full go is a cycle, and the time for one cycle is the bounce time.
explanations.description: Hang a bottle on a band and pull it down. When you let go, the stretched band pulls the bottle up. The bottle speeds up as it rises. When it reaches the middle place, the band is no longer pulling, but the bottle is moving fast, so it carries on upwards. Now the band is squashed or slack, and the bottle slows. It stops, and falls. It passes the middle place again, goes down past it, and stops at the bottom. That is one cycle. Then it all repeats. The time for one cycle is the bounce time. Scientists call it the period. The number of cycles in a second is the frequency, counted in hertz. To time a bounce fairly, do not time just one. A stopwatch cannot catch a fraction of a second well. Time ten bounces, then divide by ten. Repeat three times and use the middle time. Start the clock on a clear moment, such as the lowest point, and count the first one as nought. If the bounces die away fast, count eight instead of ten.
examples: Ten bounces take 8 seconds, so one bounce takes 0.8 seconds. The frequency is about 1.25 hertz.
A child on a swing completes one cycle each time she returns to where she started.
A guitar string's frequency is how many times it vibrates in a second. A lower note has a lower frequency.
explanations.art: A bottle on a band shown at the start, lowest point, middle and highest point, joined by an arrow loop, with a stopwatch counting ten bounces.
explanations.context: In the Bounce Time test, you time bounces carefully. This card explains what a bounce is and how to time it so the number is trustworthy.

explanations.concept: What sets the bounce time: the load and the stiffness
explanations.definition: The bounce time depends on the load and on the stiffness of the spring. A load four times bigger makes the bounce time twice as long. A spring four times stiffer makes it half as long.
explanations.description: A heavy load is harder to speed up, so it takes longer to go through each cycle. A stiff spring pulls harder for each centimetre, so it speeds the load up faster, and each cycle is quicker. The two ideas combine into one rule. The bounce time grows with the square root of the load, and shrinks with the square root of the stiffness. A square root is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives your number. The square root of 4 is 2, and the square root of 9 is 3. So four times the load makes the bounce time twice as long, and nine times the load makes it three times as long. For a spring with a stiffness of 0.5 newtons for each centimetre, a 0.25 kilogram load bounces in about 0.44 seconds, a 0.5 kilogram load in about 0.63 seconds, a 1 kilogram load in about 0.89 seconds and a 2 kilogram load in about 1.26 seconds. Notice that 0.89 is twice 0.44, because the load went up four times. Real rubber bands follow the rule only roughly, because rubber is not a perfect spring. The rule also does not depend on gravity. A load on a spring bounces at the same beat on the Moon, in space and on Earth.
examples: A schoolbag on a spring bounces slowly. A pencil box on the same spring bounces fast.
A car with a full load of passengers bounces more slowly on its springs than an empty car.
A ruler clamped at the table's edge wobbles faster when only a short part sticks out, because the short part is stiffer.
explanations.art: Three bottles of different sizes on identical bands, with the bounce time written next to each: short, medium and long.
explanations.context: In the Bounce Time test, a bigger load made each bounce take longer. This card explains the rule behind it.

explanations.concept: Why a bigger bounce does not take longer
explanations.definition: A bigger bounce has further to go, but a spring pulls harder when it is stretched further. So the load goes faster, and the two effects cancel. The bounce time stays the same.
explanations.description: Most people expect a bigger bounce to take longer. Think about it from the spring's side. Pull the bottle down 2 centimetres, and the band pulls back with a small force. Pull it down 6 centimetres, and the band pulls with three times as much. A bigger pull speeds the bottle up more. So the bottle travels three times as far, but it also goes about three times as fast. The two effects cancel, and the time for one bounce stays the same. This works as long as the spring keeps pulling in even steps, that is, as long as the pull is proportional to the stretch. Springs that do this are the reason a pendulum clock and a mass on a spring keep steady time, however big the swing. Real bounces die away slowly, but the time of each one hardly changes. When the stretch gets very large, the pull stops being proportional, and then the bounce time does change a little. Rubber bands show this a bit more than steel springs do.
examples: A swing of a pendulum clock takes the same time whether the swing is large or small, as long as it is not too large.
A bottle pulled down by 2 centimetres and a bottle pulled down by 6 centimetres bounce at about the same beat.
A guitar string vibrates at the same note, whether it is plucked hard or softly. Only the loudness changes.
explanations.art: Two bottles on bands, one with a small bounce and one with a big bounce, each with a clock showing the same time for one bounce, and arrows showing the big one going faster.
explanations.context: In the Bounce Time test, you may find that a big bounce and a small bounce take the same time. This card explains why.

explanations.definition: Every spring and load has a natural beat. If you push or shake it in time with that beat, each push adds to the movement, and the bounce grows big. This is called resonance.
explanations.description: Think of pushing a child on a swing. A swing has a natural beat. If you push at the right moment, as the swing comes back to you, each push adds to the swing, and it goes higher with only small pushes. If you push at the wrong moment, while the swing is coming towards you, you work against its movement and slow it down. A bottle on a band is the same. Move the top end of the band up and down in time with the bottle's natural beat, and tiny movements of your hand build a big bounce. Move your hand much slower or much faster than the natural beat, and the bottle hardly moves at all. A heavier bottle has a slower natural beat, so it needs a slower shake to build up. Resonance is everywhere. A radio picks one station out of thousands, because its circuit has a favourite beat that matches that station. Musical instruments ring because their strings, skins or air columns have natural beats. The same idea helps a tuning fork ring loudly in a hall. A pushed child, a tuned radio and a ringing bell are using the same idea.
examples: A parent pushes a swing in time with its beat, and a tiny push builds a high swing.
A radio tunes to one station by matching its own beat to the station's.
Soldiers marching over a bridge are told to break step, in case their steps match the bridge's natural beat. Records of some incidents of this kind exist, though they are hard to confirm.
explanations.art: A bottle on a band with a hand at the top moving up and down, drawn three times: a slow hand and a small bounce, a hand in time and a big bounce, and a fast hand and a small bounce.
explanations.context: In the Favourite Beat test, you shake a band at different beats. This card explains what you will see.

explanations.definition: A bounce gets smaller and smaller because friction inside the spring, and with the air, turns the movement's energy into a little heat and sound. This dying away is called damping.
explanations.description: A real bounce never goes on for ever. The bottle bounces smaller and smaller, and at last hangs still. Where does the movement go? Some of the energy is turned into heat inside the rubber, because the rubber chains rub against each other as they stretch. Some goes into the air as sound, and some is lost as the air rubs the bottle. Damping is often useful. A car has springs, to soak up bumps, and also dampers, called shock absorbers, to stop the springs from bouncing again and again. A shock absorber is a piston pushing oil through a narrow hole. It turns the bounce into heat. Without it, a car would keep bouncing after every pothole. Engineers choose just enough damping for each job. Too little, and the thing bounces on. Too much, and it feels hard and slow to return. A door closer, a bicycle fork and a cushion all use damping in different ways.
examples: A rubber band bounces about eight times before it hangs still. A steel spring bounces for much longer.
A car's shock absorbers stop it from bouncing along the road after a pothole.
A foam cushion absorbs a fall without bouncing the person back up.
explanations.art: A wavy line that gets smaller from left to right, with a shock absorber drawn beside it as a piston in an oil tube.
explanations.context: In the Bounce Time test, your bounces get smaller and smaller. This card explains where the movement goes.

explanations.concept: A rubber band warms up when you stretch it
explanations.definition: A stretched rubber band gives out a little heat, and it cools down again when it is let go. This is the opposite of what happens in a metal spring, and it comes from the way rubber is built.
explanations.description: Take a thick rubber band, stretch it quickly and touch it to your lip. It feels slightly warm. Hold it stretched for a few seconds, then let it go and touch it to your lip again. It feels cool. Rubber is made of long chains of molecules, tangled up like a bowl of noodles. When you stretch it, the chains straighten and line up. This is a more orderly arrangement, and as the chains line up they give out some heat. When you let go, the chains tangle up again and take heat in from their surroundings, so the band feels cool. John Gough, an English natural philosopher, noticed this around 1805. James Joule measured it carefully in 1859. The change is small, usually a few degrees at most. It is very fast, so you must stretch the band quickly, and touch it right away. The warming is one reason rubber bands do not bounce for ever. Each time they are stretched and relaxed, a small part of the movement's energy turns into heat.
examples: A rubber band feels warm on your lip right after a quick stretch, and cool right after it is released.
A car tyre warms up as it flexes on the road, partly for the same reason.
A rubber band that is stretched and let go many times in a row gets warm, like a paper clip bent back and forth.
explanations.art: A tangled mass of long chains inside a relaxed band, and a straightened set of lined-up chains inside a stretched band with small waves of heat leaving it.
explanations.context: In the Hot Lip activity, you feel a stretched band warm up. This card explains why it happens.

explanations.definition: A material that is bent or stretched again and again can break, even if each bend is small. Tiny cracks start at the weak spots and grow a little with every bend, until the material snaps. This is called fatigue.
explanations.description: Bend a paper clip once by a small angle, and it springs back. Bend it back and forth by a big angle, and after ten or so bends it snaps. The bend spot also gets warm. Each bend leaves a tiny, invisible change in the metal. After enough bends, a crack starts, and each bend makes the crack grow. This is fatigue, the tiredness of materials. It is a danger for anything that moves again and again. A bridge has thousands of lorries crossing it. A railway line takes the weight of trains. An aeroplane's body flexes with every flight. In 1954, two de Havilland Comet jet airliners broke up in the air. Investigators traced the cause to fatigue cracks that started at the corner of a window in the cabin roof. Since then, aeroplane windows have rounded corners, and engineers test and inspect for cracks. A small crack can be found early, before it grows. Fatigue is also why a spring in a pen, after years of clicking, can break.
examples: A paper clip bent back and forth snaps in about ten to twenty bends.
Two Comet jet airliners of the 1950s broke up because of fatigue cracks at a window corner, and aeroplane windows have had rounded corners ever since.
A plastic ruler bent back and forth many times gets a white line and cracks.
explanations.art: A paper clip bent back and forth at its bend, with a tiny crack growing in three drawings, ending in a break.
explanations.context: In the Tired Clip activity, you bend a clip again and again. This card explains what happens to the metal.

explanations.definition: Some things store elastic energy by being held in a curved shape. When a small push makes them flip to the opposite curve, they snap through suddenly. The Venus flytrap uses this to close her trap in about a tenth of a second.
explanations.description: Press the middle of a ruler from its ends, and it bends. Push a little more, and it suddenly flips to bend the other way. Between the two bent shapes is an unstable shape, and a small push is enough to flip it over. Engineers call this snap-through or buckling. A tape measure stays straight when you pull it out, because its curved cross-section makes it stiff. Press on the end, and it suddenly kinks. A Venus flytrap uses snap-through. Her open trap is curved outwards, held in tension like a loaded spring. When an insect touches two of the small hairs inside, she closes. She closes only if the hairs are touched twice within about twenty seconds. This is a kind of counting and remembering. The two touches release a sudden change that flips the curve of the leaves from outward to inward. The trap snaps shut. Some scientists call this an automatic response. Others point out that the plant is sensing, remembering and deciding. Researchers published their study of the snap in 2005.
examples: A tape measure stands straight when pulled out, then folds suddenly when pressed.
A Venus flytrap snaps shut on a fly in about a tenth of a second.
A popper toy, a bendy plastic cup that jumps when turned inside out, uses snap-through.
explanations.art: A flytrap leaf open with a curved shape, and the same leaf closed, with an arrow between them and two small hairs touched in turn.
explanations.context: In the Tape Measure Snap activity, you see a long thin thing fold suddenly. This card explains why, and shows a plant that uses the same trick.

explanations.definition: Because a spring's bounce time does not change with the size of the bounce, springs make good clocks. Mechanical watches use a balance spring. Quartz watches use a crystal that vibrates. The second itself is now defined by the vibrations of atoms.
explanations.description: A pendulum clock does not work on a rocking ship, which is why people needed something else. In the 1670s, Christiaan Huygens and Robert Hooke both worked on small coiled springs for watches. Such a spring pulls a tiny wheel back and forth at a steady beat. This balance spring is the reason a watch can go in a pocket and still keep time. Quartz watches use a tiny crystal of quartz, cut like a small tuning fork. It vibrates 32,768 times each second. A chip counts the beats and halves the count fifteen times to get one tick each second. Atomic clocks use something even steadier: the vibrations of caesium atoms. Since 1967, the second has been defined as exactly 9,192,631,770 of these vibrations. In each case, a springy thing with a steady natural beat is counting time for us. The steadier the beat, the better the clock. A good quartz watch is wrong by less than half a minute in a month. Atomic clocks are wrong by less than a second in millions of years.
examples: A mechanical watch has a balance spring that swings a small wheel back and forth, ticking about five times each second.
A quartz watch counts the 32,768 vibrations each second of a small crystal.
The clocks in satellites that give your phone its place on the map are atomic clocks.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a mechanical watch with its balance spring, a quartz crystal like a tiny tuning fork, and a gleaming atomic clock side by side.
explanations.context: A spring's bounce time does not change with the size of the bounce. This card shows how that fact became clocks, watches and the definition of the second.

explanations.definition: A spring and a load bounce at a beat that depends on the load and the stiffness, not on gravity. So the bounce time can show how much mass a thing has, even where nothing weighs anything.
explanations.description: In the unit on measuring forces, we saw that a bag of rice weighs less on the Moon, but is still the same bag of rice. In space, an astronaut floats, and a bathroom scale cannot weigh her, because she does not press on it. But a spring can still weigh her mass. NASA has used springy seats for this. In the 1970s, the space station Skylab had a Body Mass Measurement Device. The astronaut strapped to a seat on springs and was set bouncing. A heavier astronaut bounces more slowly, and the time of the bounce shows her mass. You can do the same on a table at home. Clamp a ruler to a table edge. Fix a lump of clay to the free end. Flick it, and count the wobbles in ten seconds. A heavier lump wobbles more slowly. If you lay the ruler flat along the table, it works the same way. Gravity is not needed, because the beat depends on the mass and the stiffness. Weighing by wobbling measures the amount of stuff, the mass, rather than the pull of a planet.
examples: An astronaut's mass is found on a spring seat by timing the bounces.
A ruler with a lump of clay wobbles more slowly than the same ruler with a small lump.
A bathroom scale gives a different number on the Moon. A wobble scale gives the same number on the Moon.
explanations.art: An astronaut strapped into a spring seat floating in a space station, with a stopwatch beside her, and a ruler with a lump of clay wobbling on a table below.
explanations.context: In the Wobble Scale project, you find the mass of a lump of clay by timing a wobble. This card explains why that works, even in space.

explanations.concept: Springs all the way down: atoms and the Sun
explanations.definition: Atoms joined by a bond can vibrate like balls on a tiny spring, billions of times in a second. Heat is the random shaking of all these tiny springs. At the other end of size, the whole Sun rings like a bell.
explanations.description: Zoom into a spring, and you meet atoms. Each atom is held in place by pulls from its neighbours. If you push an atom a little, its neighbours push it back, just like a spring. Atoms joined by a bond vibrate in and out like balls on a tiny spring. In a water molecule, the bonds vibrate about a hundred million million times each second. The warmth of a thing is the random shaking of all of these tiny springs. Light of the right colour can set the springs shaking more. Carbon dioxide, a gas in air, has bonds whose natural beat matches infrared light, the kind of light that carries heat. So the gas absorbs the heat that leaves the Earth. This is the resonance behind the greenhouse effect. At the huge end of size, the Sun is a ball of gas that oscillates. Its surface rises and falls about every five minutes, as sound waves ring through it. Scientists study these oscillations to look inside the Sun, a science called helioseismology. So the same idea, a springy thing with a natural beat, appears in a pen, in an atom and in a star.
examples: A water molecule's bonds vibrate about a hundred million million times each second.
Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared light, because the light's beat matches the beat of its bonds.
The surface of the Sun rises and falls once about every five minutes.
explanations.art: A water molecule drawn as three balls joined by springs, an arrow of infrared light, and a huge Sun with ripples rolling across its surface.
explanations.context: A spring has a natural beat, and so does an atom, and so does the Sun. This card follows springs all the way down and all the way up.

explanations.definition: A thin springy plate has natural beats too. Sand sprinkled on a plate that is vibrating at one of these beats gathers in lines where the plate stays still. Sophie Germain worked out the mathematics of this in 1816.
explanations.description: In the early 1800s, a German scientist named Ernst Chladni travelled around Europe showing something strange. He scattered sand on a thin metal plate and drew a violin bow along its edge. The plate sang, and the sand jumped into beautiful patterns of lines. The sand collects where the plate does not move. A different note gives a different pattern. In Paris, the French Academy of Sciences offered a prize for a theory that could explain the patterns. It was a hard problem, since it needed new mathematics. Sophie Germain, who had taught herself mathematics from books in her father's library, entered the contest. Women were not allowed to study at the university or to join the Academy. She entered anonymously, and her early tries did not win. After a third try, she won the prize in 1816. Her work helped found the study of how elastic bodies bend and vibrate. Her result was not perfect, and others later improved on it. But the ideas she opened up are used today to design bridges, buildings and instruments.
examples: Sand on a vibrating plate gathers into lines that shift when the note changes.
The patterns look like the ones you see on the bottom of a drum or a guitar body when they ring.
Engineers use the mathematics of vibrating plates to design the floors of bridges and the walls of aeroplanes.
explanations.art: A thin metal plate with sand arranged in a pattern of lines, and a bow drawn along its edge, with a woman in an old library at a desk working on equations.
explanations.context: A plate, like a spring, has natural beats. This card is about the woman who explained the patterns made by a singing plate.

explanations.concept: Are the smallest things tiny vibrating strings?
explanations.description: Everything we know is made of particles such as electrons and quarks. Some physicists have an idea, called string theory, that these particles are not points at all. They suggest that each one is a tiny thread of energy, and that the different particles are different notes of vibration, like the different notes of a guitar string. An electron might be one note, and a photon another. The idea is beautiful, and the mathematics holds together. But nobody has found a way to test it by experiment, because the strings would be unimaginably small. Many physicists are excited by it. Others say that a theory that cannot be tested is not yet science. It is an open question.
examples: A guitar string makes many different notes by vibrating in different ways.
String theory suggests that different particles may be different vibrations of the same kind of thread.

perspectives.explanation: The idea joins gravity and the other forces in one picture, and its mathematics is rich and consistent.
No experiment has been able to test it, and a theory that cannot be tested may be mathematics rather than a description of nature.
There are other ideas, such as loop quantum gravity, for the very small and the very early universe. It is too soon to say which, if any, is right.

explanations.art: A guitar string vibrating in three different patterns, and beside it a zoom-in of a particle drawn as a tiny vibrating loop.
explanations.context: A spring or a string can have many different beats. This card asks a bold question: could the smallest things in the universe be tiny strings, each with its own beat?

agreed.text: A spring's stiffness is the pull it needs for each centimetre it stretches, and stiffnesses add when springs sit side by side.
agreed.evidence: Hang the same packet on one band, on two bands in a row and on two bands side by side. The stretch is 10, 20 and 5 centimetres for bands of 0.5 newtons for each centimetre, which matches the rule.
agreed.context: This card is about how to put a number on how stiff a spring is.

agreed.text: The bounce time of a load on a spring depends on the load and the stiffness, and not on the size of the bounce.
agreed.evidence: Ten bounces from a 2 centimetre pull and ten bounces from a 6 centimetre pull take about the same time. Four times the load makes the bounce time about twice as long. Pendulum clocks and balance springs depend on this.
agreed.context: This card is about what sets the beat of a spring.

agreed.text: A spring and its load bounce at the same beat on Earth, on the Moon and in space.
agreed.evidence: The beat depends on the load and the stiffness, and gravity does not come into it. Astronauts on Skylab found their mass by bouncing on a spring seat.
agreed.context: This card is about why bouncing can weigh things where nothing has weight.

agreed.text: Pushing a spring in time with its natural beat builds a big movement from small pushes.
agreed.evidence: A swing pushed at the right moment goes higher and higher. A bottle on a band, with a hand moving its top end at the right beat, bounces many times as far as it does with a hand moving at other beats.
agreed.context: This card is about resonance, the idea that timing matters as much as strength.

agreed.text: Bounces die away, because some of the energy turns into heat and sound.
agreed.evidence: A bottle on a band bounces smaller and smaller until it hangs still. A stretched band warms in your hand and a paper clip that is bent back and forth warms at the bend.
agreed.context: This card is about where the movement of a bounce goes.

agreed.text: Materials that are bent again and again can break, even when each bend is small.
agreed.evidence: A paper clip bent back and forth snaps in about ten to twenty bends. In 1954, two Comet jet airliners broke up in the air, and the cause was traced to fatigue cracks that started at the corner of a window in the cabin roof.
agreed.context: This card is about why engineers test and inspect things that flex over and over.

challenging.claim: A bigger bounce takes longer than a small one.
challenging.who: Most people, who guess that a longer path takes more time.
challenging.for: A bigger bounce has further to go, and it looks slower.
challenging.against: A bigger stretch makes the spring pull harder, so the load goes faster. The two effects cancel. Ten bounces of 2 centimetres and ten bounces of 6 centimetres take about the same time.
challenging.context: Many people guess that big bounces take longer. This card looks at that idea.

challenging.claim: A heavier load makes a spring bounce faster.
challenging.who: Some people, who think a heavier thing has more push.
challenging.for: A heavier load stretches the spring further, and the spring pulls harder.
challenging.against: The spring pulls harder, but the load is also harder to speed up. The load wins. A heavier load bounces more slowly, and four times the load makes the bounce time twice as long.
challenging.context: Does a heavy load make a spring bounce faster or slower? This card looks at a common guess.

challenging.claim: A stiffer spring is a stronger spring.
challenging.who: Many people, who use 'stiff' and 'strong' for the same thing.
challenging.for: A stiff spring is hard to stretch, which feels like strength.
challenging.against: Stiff means a big pull for a small stretch. Strong means able to take a big load without breaking. A stiff rubber band can snap at a small stretch, and a soft steel spring can take a huge load. A glass rod is stiff but breaks easily.
challenging.context: Stiff and strong are not the same thing. This card looks at how they differ.

challenging.claim: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge fell in 1940 because of resonance with the wind.
challenging.for: The bridge twisted in a wind of about 65 kilometres an hour, and the movement grew until the deck broke.
challenging.against: Engineers who studied the bridge later found that the wind did not push it at its natural beat. They found that the bridge's own movement drew energy from the steady wind, an effect called flutter. This is a different effect from simple resonance.
challenging.context: A famous bridge fell in 1940. This card asks whether resonance was the cause.

challenging.claim: A spring only stores energy. It never loses any.
challenging.who: Many students who learn about ideal springs.
challenging.for: A good steel spring bounces many times and seems to give back almost all the energy.
challenging.against: No real spring is perfect. A rubber band warms up and bounces only a few times. A steel spring bounces for longer, but it too loses a little each time, to heat and sound.
challenging.context: Does a spring keep all its energy? This card looks at a tidy idea that is not quite true.

challenging.claim: Only coiled metal is a spring.
challenging.for: The word spring brings to mind a coil of wire.
challenging.against: Anything elastic acts like a spring: a ruler, a diving board, a tree branch, a tendon and even the bond between two atoms. A spring is anything that pulls back in proportion to how far it is pushed.
challenging.context: What counts as a spring? This card asks whether it has to be a coil of metal.

big_questions.q: A big bounce and a small bounce take the same time. So what does the bottle know about the size of its bounce?
big_questions.hint: Does the bottle need to know anything? What does the spring do when it is stretched further?

big_questions.q: A tiny push at the right moment builds a huge swing, and a huge push at the wrong moment does nothing. Is it the strength of a push that matters, or its timing?
big_questions.hint: Think about pushing a swing. What happens if you push as it comes towards you?

big_questions.q: Atoms in a solid behave like tiny balls on springs. So is a solid really solid, or is it a crowd of tiny vibrating things?
big_questions.hint: Zoom in on a table. Is anything still?

big_questions.q: A spring bounces at the same beat on the Moon as on Earth, but a pendulum does not. What does that tell us about what weight is?
big_questions.hint: What does the spring need in order to bounce? What does the pendulum need?

big_questions.q: Everything in a clock keeps time by repeating. Can we measure time without anything repeating?
big_questions.hint: Think of a clock. What does it count? Could you count something that never repeats?

big_questions.q: A paper clip breaks after ten bends, although each bend was small. What else in life gets tired by many small things, rather than one big thing?
big_questions.hint: Think of materials, of people and of mountains worn by rain.

big_questions.q: A Venus flytrap closes only after two touches. Is counting a thing only brains do?
big_questions.hint: What does the flytrap need to remember between the first touch and the second?

big_questions.q: Sophie Germain was not allowed in the university, but she won a major prize. What did she have that mattered more than a place at the university?
big_questions.hint: What did she need to start? A classroom, or a question, books and persistence?

big_questions.q: If every particle is a note, and the universe is a vast chord, who or what plays it?
big_questions.hint: String theory is an idea, not an answer. Can music exist without a musician?

big_questions.q: Resonance can build a huge movement from tiny pushes. Could a small change at the right moment change a lot in your own life?
big_questions.hint: Think of a small word at the right time. Is that the same as a small push at the right beat?

story.title: Push When It Comes Back
story.note: A made-up story. The lane, Saroja, Paati, Karuppasamy and the others are imagined. The science is real. Small pushes timed with the natural rocking of a vehicle on its springs and soft tyres build up a big rocking, which is how stuck vehicles are often rocked out of mud. Pushing a swing at the right moment works in the same way.
text: Saroja lived in a narrow lane near the big temple in Madurai, where the evening rain turned the road into brown soup. One Tuesday, the milk van came down the lane as the sun was setting. Its back wheel dropped into a hole where the road had been dug up for a new pipe. The van stopped with a jolt, tilted like a tired buffalo.
Karuppasamy, the driver, pressed the pedal until the engine screamed and mud flew up the wall. The wheel spun, and the hole got deeper.

People came out of their houses. Mani Anna, who sold tea at the corner, came with a cloth over his shoulder. Two college boys came, and the watchman, and Fatima Akka from the tailoring shop, her hands still dusty with chalk. 'Everyone push!' shouted the driver. They stood behind the van in a line and shoved with all their strength.

The van moved a finger's width, and then rolled back into the hole. They shoved again, groaning. It moved a finger's width, and rolled back. After ten minutes they were hot and muddy and tired, and the hole was still full of van.

Saroja watched from her verandah steps, where her little brother Kannan was swinging on the old wooden unjal. Its chains creaked softly. Every evening she pushed him, and every evening Paati, her grandmother, said the same thing from her chair: 'Don't push the swing when you feel like it. Push when it comes back to you.'

Saroja looked at the van again. Something about it looked familiar. Each time the people shoved, the van moved forward a little, and then it moved back. It was not just stuck. It was rocking, very slightly, forwards and backwards on its springs, and on its soft tyres in the soft mud. It was rocking like a slow swing.
She ran down the steps and into the lane. 'Stop!' she shouted. 'Don't push all together!' Some of the men turned and looked at her. A girl of ten, with muddy feet, in the middle of the road.

'The van is rocking,' Saroja said. 'Look! It goes forward, and then it comes back. It has its own beat, like Kannan's swing. When you all push at once, some of you push while it is coming back, and you stop each other. Push only when it comes back to you. Then push it forward.'
The college boys laughed. But Fatima Akka wiped her hands on her sari. 'Let the child try,' she said. 'Nothing else is working.'

So Saroja stood on a stone by the wall where everyone could see her. 'Wait,' she said. They waited. The van rocked forward a tiny bit, stopped, and rocked back. 'Now!' she called, just as it began to roll forward again. They all pushed together. The van lurched forward a little more than before.

'Wait.' It rolled back. 'Now!' They pushed. It went a little further. 'Wait.' 'Now!' With every push, the rocking grew. A finger's width. Two fingers. A hand. A forearm. Nobody pushed harder than before. They only pushed at the right moment.

On the eighth push, the van's back wheel climbed the lip of the hole with a loud squelch and rolled out onto the road. The lane filled with cheering. Karuppasamy jumped out of the cab, shaking his head. 'How did you know?' he asked.
Saroja shrugged. 'It's like a swing,' she said. 'Paati says you can't hurry it. You can only join it.'
From her chair on the verandah, Paati lifted one eyebrow, the way she did when she was pleased and trying not to show it.

That night, Saroja pushed Kannan on the unjal and counted slowly. One swing took about three seconds, whether he was swinging high or low. She pushed him a little at the wrong moment, and he slowed down. She pushed him a little at the right moment, and he went higher. Every time, a small push at the right moment did more than a big push at the wrong one.
story.epiphany: For the parent: every springy thing, including a swing, a vehicle on its springs and a bottle on a band, has a natural beat. A push adds to the movement only if it comes at the right moment, so that it goes with the movement and not against it. Many small pushes in time build a big movement. This is called resonance. Saroja noticed that the van was rocking, worked out its beat, and called the pushes at the right moment, while the grown-ups pushed hard but at random.
ask: Why do many small pushes at the right moments move a swing higher than a few big pushes at the wrong moments?
What is a natural beat, and what two things set the natural beat of a bottle on a band?
When you push a swing as it is coming towards you, what happens to the swing? Why?
Why does a heavier swing, with a heavier rider, have a slower natural beat?
Name another springy thing, other than a swing or a vehicle, where timing the pushes could make a small push build a big movement.
art: A narrow lane near a South Indian temple at dusk, wet from rain, a milk van tilted with its back wheel in a muddy hole.
A line of grown-ups pushing at the back of the van, mud splashing, with a girl watching from a verandah and a boy on a wooden swing beside her.
The girl standing on a stone by the wall, one hand raised, calling to the pushers, while the van rocks forward.
The van's back wheel climbing out of the hole while people cheer, and the girl smiling at her grandmother on the verandah.

games.title: Beat Match: longer, shorter or the same?
games.context: This is a card game about the beat of springs. Each card describes a bouncing thing and one change. Players guess how the bounce time changes, and then check the back of the card.

setup.art: A table with a pile of 24 cards face down, eight word tokens in a row, and a pencil and paper for each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them face down.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while two other players put a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Each other player picks a token.

setup.art: The back of a card with the answer, and the players turning their tokens over together.
setup.caption: 3. Everyone turns over their token. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a bouncing thing and a change on the front, and the answer with the reason on the back

items.f: A bottle bounces on a band. You pull it down twice as far before letting go. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: The same. A bigger bounce goes faster, so the time does not change.

items.f: A bottle bounces on a band. You hang a bottle that is 4 times heavier. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Twice as long. The square root of 4 is 2.

items.f: A load bounces on a band. You hang a load that is 9 times heavier. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Three times as long. The square root of 9 is 3.

items.f: A load bounces on a band. You change to a spring that is 4 times stiffer, with the same load. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Half as long. A stiffer spring pulls harder and speeds the load up faster.

items.f: A load hangs on one band. You use two identical bands side by side instead, with the same load. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Shorter. The pair is twice as stiff, so the bounce is faster.

items.f: A load hangs on one band. You use two identical bands in a row instead, with the same load. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Longer. The pair is half as stiff, so the bounce is slower.

items.f: A bottle on a band is taken from the Earth to the Moon. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: The same. A spring's beat does not depend on gravity.

items.f: A pendulum is taken from the Earth to the Moon. How does its swing time change?
items.b: Longer. A pendulum depends on gravity, and gravity is weaker on the Moon.

items.f: A bottle bounces on a band. Half of the water is poured out. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Shorter. A lighter load is easier to speed up.

items.f: A car bounces on its springs. Compare a car full of people with the empty car. How is the bounce time of the full car?
items.b: Longer. The full car has more load on the same springs.

items.f: A ruler is clamped at a table edge with 10 centimetres sticking out. Now 20 centimetres stick out. How does the wobble time change?
items.b: Longer. A longer part is softer, so it wobbles more slowly.

items.f: A thin rubber band is replaced by a thick one of the same length, with the same load. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Shorter. A thick band is stiffer.

items.f: A load hangs on one band. You use four identical bands in a row instead. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Twice as long. Four in a row is four times as soft.

items.f: A load hangs on one band. You use four identical bands side by side instead. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Half as long. Four side by side is four times as stiff.

items.f: A load of 1 kilogram bounces in 1 second on a band. A load of 0.25 kilograms hangs on it instead. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Half as long, which is 0.5 seconds. The load is 4 times lighter.

items.f: A load of 1 kilogram bounces in 1 second on a band. A load of 4 kilograms hangs on it instead. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Twice as long, which is 2 seconds.

items.f: A bottle bounces on a band, and its bounce slowly dies away. Does the time for one bounce change as the bounces get smaller?
items.b: The same. Smaller bounces take the same time as bigger ones.

items.f: A guitar string is plucked hard, and then softly. How does the time for one vibration change?
items.b: The same. Only the loudness changes.

items.f: A guitar string is tightened, so it is stiffer. How does the time for one vibration change?
items.b: Shorter. A tighter string is stiffer, so it makes a higher note.

items.f: A load bounces on a spring. You hang a load 16 times heavier. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Four times as long. The square root of 16 is 4.

items.f: A load bounces on a band. You hang a load 9 times lighter. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: A third as long. The square root of 9 is 3, and 9 times lighter divides the time by 3.

items.f: A watch's balance spring is changed to a stiffer one, with the same small wheel. How does its beat time change?
items.b: Shorter. A stiffer spring makes the wheel swing faster, so the watch runs fast.

items.f: A bus bounces on its springs. Half of the people get off. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: Shorter. The load is lighter.

items.f: The same bottle and band are tested on the ground floor and on the tenth floor of a building. How does the bounce time change?
items.b: The same. A spring's beat does not depend on the height.

printables.title: 8 answer tokens: Longer, Shorter, The same, Twice as long, Half as long, Three times as long, Four times as long and A third as long

rules: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
One player is the reader. The reader turns over the top card and reads the front aloud. The back stays hidden.
Every other player puts one token face down, to show how the bounce time changes.
Everyone turns their token over together.
The reader reads the back. A right answer scores 1 point. A right answer with a good reason scores 2 points.
After every 4 cards, the next player becomes the reader. With two players, swap after every card.
After all 24 cards, add up the points. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: read a card, choose your token, then check the back. There are 24 points to win. Try to beat your own score next time.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards. Read the tokens aloud. Say that the beat of a spring is the time for one bounce.
flow.say: We will guess how the bounce time changes. The bounce time is the time for one bounce. Longer means slower. Shorter means faster.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. A bounce time is the time for one bounce.
flow.context: This is the first step of Beat Match. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first 8 cards slowly. After each card, read the back aloud. After the second card, ask the question below.
flow.say: I read the card. You pick a token and say why. Now we turn them over together. Who can say why?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Say why. Check the back.

ask.q: What makes a bounce time longer, and what makes it shorter?
good: A heavier load makes it longer.
A stiffer spring makes it shorter.
The size of the bounce does not change it.

flow.context: In this step of Beat Match, you play the first eight cards and learn how the load and the stiffness change the beat.

flow.do: Play 8 more cards. Look for the cards where the answer is the same. Ask why each one does not change the bounce time.
flow.say: Look at the cards where the answer is the same. What did we change? What did we not change? Why does the bounce time stay the same?
flow.kid: Play 8 more cards. Which cards have the answer The same? Why?
flow.think: On the Moon, a spring bounces at the same beat. Why does a pendulum not?

check.q: A bottle is bounced on a band. You pull it down twice as far. What happens to the bounce time?
check.why: A bigger bounce has further to go, but the band pulls harder, so the bottle goes faster. The two effects cancel. A doubled time would only happen if the bottle went at the same speed. A halved time would mean the bottle went twice as fast over the same path.

flow.context: In this step of Beat Match, you play more cards and see why some changes do not change the beat.

flow.do: Play the last 8 cards. For the cards with square roots, write the load change, and the square root of it, before you pick your token.
flow.say: For the heavy and light cards, work out the square root of the change. Four times the load means twice the time. What does nine times the load mean?
flow.kid: Play the last 8 cards. For heavy and light cards, find the square root.

check.q: A load bounces in 2 seconds on a spring. You hang a load 4 times lighter. What is the new bounce time?
check.why: A load 4 times lighter divides the time by the square root of 4, which is 2. So 2 seconds becomes 1 second. The answer 8 seconds multiplies when it should divide. The answer 0.5 seconds divides by 4 instead of 2.

flow.context: In this step of Beat Match, you play the last cards and use square roots to find the new time.

flow.do: Add up the points. Pick the card that surprised you most, and say what you learned.
flow.say: Who has the most points? Which card surprised you the most, and why?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which card surprised you most? Why?
flow.think: If you could make a bounce time shorter, what would you change in a bottle on a band?
flow.context: This is the last step of Beat Match. You add up the points and think about what sets the beat.

experiments.title: Bounce Time: what changes how fast a spring bounces?
experiments.question: Does a bigger bounce take longer than a small bounce? And what happens to the bounce time when the load is four times heavier?
experiments.predict: Before you start, make two guesses. First, will a big bounce take longer, shorter or the same time as a small bounce? Second, how will the bounce time change if the load is four times heavier? Say why you think so for each guess.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same chain of two bands, the same stick and the same height every time. To test the size of the bounce, only the pull-down changes. To test the load, the pull-down stays at 4 centimetres and only the load changes. Time ten bounces each time, starting the clock at the moment you let go. Do every test three times, because one timing can be a fluke.

materials.item: 2 wide rubber bands, about 6 millimetres wide, linked together like a chain

a long straight stick about 1 metre long (a mop stick, bamboo pole or curtain rod), two heavy chairs, masking tape and a soft cushion. No stick? Tie the top band to a window grill bar or a strong hook instead.
a strong carrier or cloth bag with handles, to hang from the bands (double a thin polythene bag so it cannot tear)

loads of 250, 500 and 1000 grams: sealed packets of rice, sugar or dal from the kirana that say their weight on the pack (a 250 g, a 500 g and a 1 kg, or two 500 g). No scale is needed. Or fill a plastic bottle with water: 250 ml weighs about 250 g.
a phone or clock that shows seconds, and a 30 centimetre ruler
paper and a pencil

experiments.safety: Stand to the side and keep your face away from the bands, in case one snaps. Never use more than 1 kilogram of load. Keep the cushion on the floor under the bag, so that nothing lands on your feet. Put a heavy book on each chair seat so the chairs cannot tip, and keep a grown-up in the room.
experiments.record: Write the time for ten bounces for each test and each try. For each test, find the middle time and divide it by ten to get the time of one bounce. Write your claims for the size of the bounce and for the load, with your evidence and your reasons.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you hang a bag of rice on two rubber bands and time its bounces. You change the size of the bounce and then the load, and see what changes the beat.

setup.art: A long stick lying across the backs of two chairs and taped down, with two linked rubber bands hanging from the middle and a carrier bag with a packet of rice at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Make the rig. Hang the bag from the two linked bands.

setup.art: A hand pulling the bag down 2 centimetres, with a ruler held beside it, and a phone stopwatch ready.
setup.caption: 2. Pull the bag down 2 centimetres. Let go and time ten bounces.

setup.art: The same bag pulled down 6 centimetres, with the ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the bag down 6 centimetres. Time ten bounces again.

setup.art: Three bags of rice of different sizes labelled 250 grams, 500 grams and 1000 grams, hanging one after another from the same bands.
setup.caption: 4. Change the load to 250 grams, 500 grams and 1000 grams. Time ten bounces each.

setup.art: A table of times with a row for each test, and a sentence below each that begins I think, I saw, because.
setup.caption: 5. Find the middle time for each test. Write your claim, evidence and reasoning.

flow.do: Show your child the bands, the bag and the rice. Ask for two guesses and the reasons. Write them at the top of the page. With one child, the parent holds the ruler and the clock while the child pulls and counts. With 2 to 4 children, one rig is enough. One pulls, one holds the ruler, one times and one writes. Swap after each load.
flow.say: We will bounce a bag of rice on two bands. Will a big bounce take longer than a small bounce? And if the rice is four times heavier, how will the bounce time change? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A bag bounces on bands. Does a big bounce take longer? What if the bag is four times heavier? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think a big bounce will take that long?
good: A big bounce goes further, so it takes longer.
A big bounce is faster, so it takes the same time.
A bigger pull makes the bag go faster.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children say a big bounce takes longer, and a heavier load takes twice as long or four times as long. Write whatever they say with the reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bounce Time test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Lay the stick across the backs of two heavy chairs, about 1 metre apart. Tape both ends down. Link the two bands like a chain and tie one end to the middle of the stick. Hang the bag from the other end. Put the 500 gram packet in the bag.
flow.say: Link the two bands like a chain. Tie the top band to the stick, and hang the bag from the bottom band. Put one packet in the bag. The bag should hang clear of the floor.
flow.kid: Link the two bands. Tie them to the stick. Hang the bag. Put one packet in.
flow.parent: The bag with the packet should hang at least 10 centimetres off the floor. If the bands stretch so far that they look thin and pale, or longer than three times their relaxed length, add a third band to share the pull, and use that chain for the whole test. Wait for the bag to settle before you start.

check.q: Why do we use the same bands for all the tests?
options: So that only the thing we change can alter the bounce time
So that the bands do not get tired
So that the bag stays dry
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the bands were different, we would not know whether the load or the band changed the bounce time. Tired bands and dry bags are not the reason.

flow.context: In this step, you build the rig with two bands in a row and a bag of rice.

flow.do: With the 500 gram packet in the bag, pull the bag down 2 centimetres and let go. Time ten bounces. Do this three times. Then pull the bag down 6 centimetres and time ten bounces three times. Write all six times.
flow.say: Pull the bag down exactly 2 centimetres, let go and count ten bounces. Stop the clock on the tenth. Do it three times. Then pull down 6 centimetres and do it three times more.
flow.kid: Pull the bag down 2 cm. Let go. Time ten bounces. Do it three times. Then 6 cm.

ask.q: What do you notice about the two sets of times?
good: They are about the same.
The big bounces took about the same time as the small ones.
The big bounces went faster.

flow.parent: Expect about 7 to 11 seconds for ten bounces with the 500 gram load. The 2 centimetre and 6 centimetre times should be within a second or so of each other. Rubber bands damp the bounce, so count the first ten and stop. If the bounce dies away before ten, count eight and divide by eight. Start the clock when you let go, and call out the count as the bag passes the lowest point. Pull the bag straight down by the distance on the ruler, and let go without pushing. If it swings sideways, catch it and start again. Rubber bands vary, so your times may differ from these; what matters is the comparison between your own tests.

check.q: Ten bounces from a 2 cm pull took 8.2 seconds, and ten bounces from a 6 cm pull took 8.4 seconds. What does this suggest?
options: The size of the bounce hardly changes the bounce time
A bigger bounce is much faster
A bigger bounce is much slower
check.why: 8.2 and 8.4 seconds differ by only 0.2 seconds, which is less than the timing error. So the size of the bounce does not change the bounce time. A big difference would show up as seconds, not tenths of a second.

flow.context: In this step, you time ten bounces for a small pull and a big pull, three times each.

flow.do: Pull the bag down 4 centimetres every time. Time ten bounces three times with 250 grams, three times with 500 grams and three times with 1000 grams. Write all nine times.
flow.say: Now we change the load. Use 250 grams, then 500 grams, then 1000 grams. Pull down 4 centimetres each time. Time ten bounces, three times for each load.
flow.kid: Pull down 4 cm each time. Use 250 g, 500 g and 1000 g. Time ten bounces, three times each.
flow.think: How much longer do you expect 1000 grams to take than 250 grams?
flow.parent: Typical times for ten bounces, though bands differ: roughly 5 to 8 seconds for 250 grams, 7 to 11 seconds for 500 grams and 10 to 16 seconds for 1000 grams. The 1000 gram time should be longer than the 250 gram time by a factor of about 2, since 1000 grams is four times 250 grams. Rubber bands stiffen when they are stretched a lot, so the factor is often a little under 2, perhaps 1.5 to 2.1. Any clear increase of about this size supports the idea. Keep the bag low over the cushion, and take the 1000 gram load off at once if the bands look thin and pale.

check.q: Ten bounces took 5 seconds with 250 grams. About how long do you expect for 1000 grams?
check.why: 1000 grams is 4 times 250 grams. The square root of 4 is 2, so the time doubles to about 10 seconds. The answer 20 seconds would be right if the time grew four times. The answer 5 seconds would be right if the load did not matter.

flow.context: In this step, you time ten bounces with three different loads, to see how the load changes the beat.

flow.do: Find the middle time for each test. Divide each by ten for one bounce. Look at your first guesses. Write three sentences for the size of the bounce, and three for the load: claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What did you think? What did you find? Why did the load change the bounce time, but not the size of the bounce? Write what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: Find the middle time for each test. Was your guess right? Write what you think, what you saw and why.

ask.q: Why does the size of the bounce not change the time, when the load does?
good: A bigger pull speeds the bag up, so the bounce takes the same time.
A heavier bag is harder to speed up.
The spring and the load set the beat.

flow.parent: The ratio of the 1000 gram time to the 250 gram time is the key number. A ratio near 2 matches the square root rule, and a ratio of 1.5 to 2.1 is typical for rubber. The size of the bounce should change the time very little. If your results are very different, check that every test used the same pull-down and the same bands.
flow.context: In this step, you find the middle times and write your claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: The Favourite Beat: which shake builds the biggest bounce?
experiments.question: If you move the top end of a band up and down at different speeds, which speed makes a hanging bag bounce the most? And does the best speed change when the bag is heavier?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will a slow shake, a medium shake or a fast shake make the bag bounce the most? Will a heavier bag want a faster or a slower shake? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bands, the same bag and the same size of hand movement every time, about 2 centimetres up and down. Only the speed of your hand changes. Shake at each speed for ten ups and downs, and measure the biggest bounce of the bag against the ruler. Then change only the load.
results_table: Time for one hand movement up and down (s)
Biggest bounce of the bag with 500 g (cm)
Biggest bounce of the bag with 1000 g (cm)

materials.item: the two linked rubber bands and the carrier bag from the Bounce Time test
a 500 gram packet and a second 500 gram packet of rice, or a bottle of water in the bag (500 ml weighs about 500 g)
a 30 centimetre ruler, and a helper to read it (a phone video of the bag beside the ruler also works)
a phone with a free metronome app, or the phone stopwatch and a helper to call the time (see the steps)
a soft cushion for the floor

experiments.safety: Stand to the side and keep your face away from the bands. Keep the cushion on the floor under the bag. Never use more than 1 kilogram of load. A grown-up stays in the room, and a bag that swings wildly is caught and stopped, not hit.
experiments.record: Write the biggest bounce for each hand speed, once for 500 grams and once for 1000 grams. Circle the speed that gave the biggest bounce each time. Write what you found, and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you hold the top end of a band and move it up and down at different speeds. You find the speed that makes the hanging bag bounce the most, which is the bag's favourite beat.

setup.art: A child holding the top of two linked rubber bands in one hand, a carrier bag with a packet hanging from the bottom, and a ruler held beside the bag by a helper.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the top of the bands. Hang the bag with 500 grams. A helper holds the ruler beside the bag.

setup.art: A phone with a metronome app showing 60 beats a minute, and the child's hand moving up and down once for each tick.
setup.caption: 2. Move your hand up and down once for each tick of the metronome.

setup.art: A table with six rows, one for each hand speed, and the bag's biggest bounce written beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Try six speeds, from slow to fast. Write the biggest bounce for each.

setup.art: The bag changed to 1000 grams and the same test repeated, with a bigger gap in the best speed.
setup.caption: 4. Change to 1000 grams. Find the best speed again.

flow.do: Show your child the bands and the bag. Say that you will shake the top end of the bands at different speeds. Write the guess and the reason. With one child, the parent is the helper. With 2 to 4 children: one shakes, one reads the ruler, one calls the time or watches the metronome, one writes. Swap after each load.
flow.say: I will hold the top of the bands and move my hand up and down, a small amount. Which speed will make the bag bounce the most, slow, medium or fast? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Move the top of the bands up and down. Which speed makes the bag bounce most? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that speed will make the biggest bounce?
good: The fastest hand will make the biggest bounce.
A speed in the middle matches the bag's own beat.
Slow shaking makes the biggest bounce, because the bag can follow.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think the faster the hand, the bigger the bounce. Write down what they say.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Favourite Beat test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Hang the 500 gram bag from the bands in your hand. Let it bounce on its own and time ten bounces. Divide by ten for the time of one bounce. Divide 60 by that to get the beats each minute.
flow.say: First we find the bag's own beat. Let it bounce on its own, and time ten bounces. Divide by ten. Now divide 60 by that to get beats each minute.
flow.kid: Let the bag bounce on its own. Time ten bounces. Divide by ten.
flow.parent: If you did the Bounce Time test, you already have this number. For ten bounces in 7.5 seconds, one bounce takes 0.75 seconds, and 60 divided by 0.75 is 80 beats each minute. Write it down. This is the bag's natural beat, the one to look for later.
flow.context: In this step, you find the natural beat of the bag on the bands. You will look for it when you shake.

flow.do: Hold the top of the bands. Move your hand up and down about 2 centimetres, once for each tick. Use 30, 40, 60, 80, 100 and 150 ticks each minute. Do ten ups and downs at each speed. The helper reads the biggest bounce of the bag against the ruler.
flow.say: Move your hand up and down once for each tick. Keep the movement small, about 2 centimetres. After ten ups and downs, the helper tells us how big the bag's bounce got. Then we speed up.
flow.kid: Move your hand up and down to the ticks. Ten times at each speed. How big does the bag bounce?

ask.q: At which speed did the bag bounce the most?
good: At the speed close to the bag's own beat.
Not the fastest, and not the slowest.
At about the speed we measured in the last step.

flow.parent: The bag should bounce more than the hand moves when the beat is close to its own, perhaps 4 to 10 centimetres for a 2 centimetre hand movement, though rubber bands vary. At a much slower beat, the bag just follows the hand. At a much faster beat, it hardly moves at all. Rubber damps the bounce, so the best speed is a range rather than a single value. Read the biggest bounce as the distance between the highest and lowest place of the bottom of the bag. Hang the top loop over a pencil that you hold, so that the band cannot slip off your finger. No metronome? Use the stopwatch: the helper says go and stop, and you must finish ten ups and downs in 20 seconds (30 a minute), 15 seconds (40), 10 seconds (60), 7.5 seconds (75-80), 6 seconds (100) or 4 seconds (150).

check.q: The bag's own beat is 80 beats a minute. At which hand speed do you expect the biggest bounce?
options: The fastest speed, 150 beats a minute
The slowest speed, 30 beats a minute
check.why: A push in time with the bag's own beat adds to the movement each time, so the bounce grows big. Pushing much faster or much slower works against the bag part of the time, and the bounce stays small.

flow.context: In this step, you shake the bands at six speeds and measure the bounce each time.

flow.do: Add the second packet, so that the bag holds 1000 grams. Ask your child to guess whether the best speed is faster or slower. Test the same six speeds. Write the biggest bounce for each.
flow.say: Now the bag is twice as heavy. Will its favourite beat be faster or slower? Test the same six speeds and find out.
flow.kid: Make the bag heavier. Will its favourite beat be faster or slower? Test it.
flow.think: Why would a heavier bag want a slower shake?
flow.parent: A heavier load has a slower natural beat, about 0.7 times the beat of the 500 gram load, since the square root of 2 is about 1.4. So the best speed should drop from about 80 beats a minute to about 57. The nearest speeds to test are 60 and 40, and 60 will probably give the biggest bounce, though with soft bands the two may be close. If so, say that the best speed is between them.
flow.context: In this step, you change the load and look for the new favourite beat.

flow.do: Look at your table. Circle the biggest bounce in each column. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning about the favourite beat and the load.
flow.say: What did you find? Which speed made the biggest bounce for each bag? Why does a push at the right beat build a big bounce, and a push at the wrong beat do very little?
flow.kid: Circle the biggest bounce in each column. What did you find? Why?

ask.q: Why did the heavier bag have a different favourite beat?
good: A heavier bag bounces more slowly on its own, so it wants a slower shake.
The bag's own beat changed.
The push must match the bag's own beat.

flow.think: If you shook much harder at the wrong beat, would the bounce grow? Try it.
flow.context: In this step, you write what you found about the favourite beat and the load.

activities.title: The Stiffness League: which stretchy thing is stiffest?

materials.item: 4 stretchy things: a wide rubber band, a thin rubber band, a hair tie and the spring from a retractable pen
a sealed 250 gram packet of rice, sugar or dal in a small bag, so that no scale is needed (a load of about 2.5 newtons). A second 250 gram packet for the doubling test.
a hook, nail, window grill or door handle to hang things from, and a 30 centimetre ruler
squared paper, a pencil and a calculator or paper for dividing

activities.safety: A grown-up takes the spring out of the pen, because it can spring out and the small parts are easy to lose. Count the pieces back afterwards, and keep them from the youngest child's mouth. Keep the load low over a cushion, and stop if a band looks thin and pale.

schedule.what: Guess the order of stiffness. Hang the load on each thing and measure the extension. Work out the stiffness. Draw a bar chart. Then double the load on two of the things.

activities.record: A table with each thing, its relaxed length, its length with the load, its extension and its stiffness. A bar chart of the stiffness of the four things. The extension of the spring and the wide band with 250 grams and with 500 grams.
activities.context: In this activity, you hang the same load on four stretchy things and measure how far each stretches. You work out which is the stiffest and which is the softest.

setup.art: Four stretchy things in a row on a table: a wide rubber band, a thin rubber band, a hair tie and a pen spring.
setup.caption: 1. Line up the four things. Guess which is stiffest.

setup.art: A pen spring hanging from a hook with a small bag of rice at the bottom and a ruler beside it showing the stretched length.
setup.caption: 2. Hang the load on each thing in turn. Measure its length before and after.

setup.art: A bar chart with four bars of different heights labelled with the four things, and a stiffness number above each.
setup.caption: 3. Work out each stiffness. Draw a bar for each.

flow.do: Line up the four things. Ask your child to guess the order, from softest to stiffest, and to say why. Write the guess down.
