With one child, the parent measures while the child hangs and writes. With 2 to 4 children, each child tests a different thing, then everyone shares the numbers and draws the chart.
flow.say: Pull each thing gently with your fingers. Which feels softest and which feels stiffest? Put them in order and say why.
flow.kid: Pull each thing gently. Put them in order, softest to stiffest. Why?

ask.q: How can you tell which thing is stiffest?
good: It is the hardest to stretch.
It needs the biggest pull for the same stretch.
It stretches the least under the same load.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Children often say the biggest thing is the stiffest. Write the guess down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Stiffness League. You guess the order before you test.

flow.do: Measure the relaxed length of the first thing. Hang the 250 gram bag from it and wait for it to stop moving. Measure the new length. Take away the first to get the extension. Do this for all four.
flow.say: Measure the relaxed length. Hang the bag and wait. Measure again. The extension is the second length minus the first. Do this for each thing.
flow.kid: Measure the length. Hang the bag. Measure again. Take away the first number.
flow.parent: The load is the same for every thing, which is what makes this a fair test. Measure each thing from the same two places, for example from the hook to the bottom of the knot. A grown-up should take the spring out of the pen. A pen spring may stretch very little, perhaps 1 or 2 centimetres, so measure it carefully. Hang the load gently, do not drop it. Wait about 10 seconds, because a band creeps a little longer. Measure a band or a hair tie as a loop, from end to end, lying relaxed.

check.q: Why must the load be the same for all four things?
options: So that the differences in stretch come from the things, not from the load
So that the bag does not get tired
So that the things all have the same length
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the load changed, we could not tell whether a bigger stretch came from a softer thing or from a bigger load.

flow.context: In this step, you hang the same load on each stretchy thing and measure how far it stretches.

flow.do: Work out each stiffness. Divide 2.5 newtons by the extension in centimetres. Draw a bar chart with four bars. Then hang a second 250 gram packet too (500 grams in all) on the pen spring and on the wide band. Does the stretch double?
flow.say: The load is 2.5 newtons. Divide it by the extension in centimetres. A bigger answer means a stiffer thing. Draw a bar for each one.
flow.kid: Divide 2.5 by each extension. A bigger answer is stiffer. Draw a bar for each.
flow.parent: For example, an extension of 5 centimetres gives 2.5 divided by 5, which is 0.5 newtons for each centimetre. Typical values, which will differ with your things: a pen spring 1 to 3, a wide band 0.3 to 1. A thin band is usually softer than a wide band of the same length. With 500 grams, a pen spring stretches about twice as far as with 250 grams, because a spring follows the rule that double the pull gives double the stretch. A rubber band may stretch more or less than double, because it is not so regular. Say what you saw, whatever it is.

check.q: A thing stretches 5 cm under 2.5 N. A second thing stretches 1 cm under 2.5 N. Which is stiffer, and how many times?
check.why: The second thing stretches 5 times less under the same load, so it is 5 times as stiff. Its stiffness is 2.5 newtons for each centimetre, and the first is 0.5. The first is the softer one.

flow.context: In this step, you turn your extensions into stiffness numbers and draw a bar chart.

flow.do: Look at the chart. Compare it with your first guess. Ask your child which thing surprised them most.
flow.say: Was the order what you guessed? Which thing surprised you most? What would you use the stiffest thing for, and the softest?
flow.kid: Was your order right? Which thing surprised you most?
flow.think: If you hang the same load on two bands side by side, how stiff is the pair?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Stiffness League. You compare the results with your guess.

activities.title: Hot Lip: the band that warms when you stretch it

materials.item: 3 or 4 thick rubber bands, about 1 centimetre wide, new and with no cracks (the thick kind from a kirana or stationery shop, a few rupees each), and a coin to toss
a clock that shows seconds

activities.safety: Do not do this if you are allergic to rubber. Each child uses their own band, because it touches the lip. Hold the band in both hands, stretch it only to about three times its length, point it away from the eyes, and never let go of it near your face. Old or sun-dried bands snap more easily, so stop if a band looks thin or cracked.

schedule.what: Stretch a band quickly and feel it on your lip. Hold it stretched, let it go and feel it again. Try a slow stretch. Then a blind test with a partner.

activities.record: A table with three tests: a quick stretch, a held stretch then a release, and a slow stretch. For each, write warm, cool or no change. A blind-test score out of 6.
activities.context: In this activity, you stretch a rubber band and feel its temperature change against the skin of your lip. You find that a stretched band warms up and cools when released.

setup.art: A child holding a thick rubber band in both hands and quickly stretching it to three times its length.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the band against your lip. Stretch it quickly and feel it.

setup.art: The same band, held stretched for five seconds, then loosened, then touched to the lip again.
setup.caption: 2. Hold it stretched for 5 seconds. Let it relax and feel it again.

setup.art: A band being stretched very slowly over thirty seconds and touched to the lip.
setup.caption: 3. Try again, but stretch it very slowly. Is it still warm?

flow.do: Show your child the thick band. Ask whether it will feel warm, cool or the same on the lip after a quick stretch. Write the guess.
flow.say: I will stretch the band and touch it to my lip. Will it feel warm, cool or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stretch the band quickly. Touch it to your lip. Warm, cool or the same? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the band might change its temperature?
good: Stretching it is hard work, so it gets warm.
Rubbing inside it makes heat.
It will feel the same, because I am only stretching it.

flow.context: This is the first step of Hot Lip. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Hold the band against your upper lip. Stretch it quickly to about three times its length. Feel it. Hold it stretched for 5 seconds, and then relax it quickly against the lip and feel it again.
flow.say: Hold the band to your lip. Stretch it fast, to three times its length. Is it warm? Hold it stretched for five seconds. Now let it relax and touch your lip again. Is it cool?
flow.kid: Stretch the band fast. Feel it on your lip. Hold, then relax it. Feel again.
flow.parent: The change is small, about a degree or a few degrees, but a lip is sensitive. Stretch the band as fast as you can, and touch it within a second. The relaxed band should feel cool. If you feel nothing, try a thicker band or stretch it further. In hot weather the band is already near body warmth, so the warm feel is small and the cool feel after release is easier to notice. Work in the coolest room.

check.q: A band feels warm right after it is stretched and cool right after it is let go. What is the best explanation?
options: Stretching lines up the rubber chains and gives out heat. Relaxing lets them tangle, which takes heat in
The band is cold on the inside
The lip makes the band warm
check.why: In a stretched band, the long chains line up and give out a little heat. When the band relaxes, the chains tangle again and take in heat from around. A cold inside would not make it warm when stretched. The lip would warm the band the same way in both tests.

flow.context: In this step, you stretch the band fast and feel it warm up, and then relax it and feel it cool.

flow.do: Stretch another band very slowly, over about 30 seconds, and touch it to your lip. Compare this with the quick stretch. Write what you find.
flow.say: Now stretch the band very slowly, over half a minute. Touch it to your lip. Is it as warm as before?
flow.kid: Stretch a band very slowly. Touch it to your lip. Is it as warm?
flow.think: Why would a slow stretch feel less warm than a fast stretch?
flow.parent: A slow stretch gives the heat time to spread into the air and your fingers, so it hardly feels warm. This is one reason you must be quick.
flow.context: In this step, you stretch the band slowly and compare it with the quick stretch.

flow.do: Blind test. One child shuts their eyes. Their partner tosses a coin six times in secret. On heads, the partner stretches the band quickly and touches the child's lip. On tails, the partner touches it with the unstretched band. The child says warm or no change each time. Count how many are right out of 6. With one child, the parent is the partner. With 2 to 4 children, take turns, with one as the coin-tosser and one as the writer.
flow.say: Close your eyes. I will touch the band to your lip, sometimes stretched and sometimes not. Tell me warm or no change. Let us see how many you get right out of 6.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Say warm or no change. How many are right out of 6?
flow.parent: Pure guessing gets about 3 right out of 6. A score of 5 or 6 shows that the warmth is real and not imagined. If the score is low, stretch further and faster, touch within a second, and say honestly that the warming is small.
flow.think: Why do we use a coin and closed eyes?
flow.context: In this step of Hot Lip, you check that the warmth is real by a blind test.

activities.title: Tired Clip: how many bends before it breaks?

materials.item: 8 steel paper clips of the same size and make, plain, with no plastic coating (a box of 100 costs about Rs 10 to 20)
a plate or tray to catch the pieces, and a protective pair of glasses if you have them
paper and a pencil. Draw a 90 degree corner and a 45 degree line on the paper to hold the clip against as a guide.

activities.safety: A grown-up bends the clips, or watches closely if an older child does it. The broken ends are sharp and can fly. Hold the clip low, over the tray, and keep your face away. The bend gets warm, so touch it gently. Count the pieces and throw them away safely, out of reach of small children.

schedule.what: Bend a clip once and see it spring back or stay bent. Bend 3 clips back and forth by 90 degrees and 3 by 45 degrees. Count bends to break. Compare.

activities.record: A table with the angle of bend, the number of bends before the clip broke, and whether the bend felt warm.
activities.context: In this activity, you bend paper clips back and forth until they break. You find that a small bend many times can do what one big bend cannot, and that the bend gets warm.

setup.art: A paper clip bent slightly and springing back, and the same clip bent a lot and staying bent.
setup.caption: 1. Bend a clip a little and let go. Then bend it a lot and let go.

setup.art: A grown-up bending a paper clip back and forth by about 90 degrees over a tray, a child counting aloud.
setup.caption: 2. Bend a clip back and forth by about 90 degrees. Count the bends until it breaks.

setup.art: A second paper clip bent back and forth by a smaller angle of about 45 degrees.
setup.caption: 3. Bend another clip by a smaller angle. Count the bends again.

flow.do: A grown-up bends one clip a little and lets go, and then bends another a lot and lets go. Ask your child what happened in each case. Ask them to guess how many back and forth bends it takes to break a clip. First open each clip out into a straight wire, gently. Then every clip is bent at a fresh spot in the middle. With one child, the parent bends and the child counts. With 2 to 4 children, one counts, one touches the bend, one writes.
flow.say: The first clip sprang back. The second stayed bent. Now I will bend a clip back and forth. How many bends do you think it will take to break? Why?
flow.kid: One bend: the clip springs back or stays bent. How many bends to break it?

ask.q: Why do you think the clip will break after that many bends?
good: Each bend wears it out a little.
It needs a lot of bends, because a clip is tough.
It will break at the first big bend.

flow.parent: A small bend stays inside the elastic limit and the clip springs back. A big bend goes past the limit and the clip stays bent. Do not correct the guess. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tired Clip. You see the difference between a small bend and a big bend, and you guess.

flow.do: A grown-up bends a clip wire back and forth by about 90 degrees against the paper guide. One bend each way counts as one. The child counts aloud. Touch the bend lightly between bends. Stop when the clip breaks. Do this with 3 clips.
flow.say: I bend the clip back, and then forward. That is one bend. You count out loud. Touch the bend lightly. Is it warm? Stop when it breaks.
flow.kid: Count each bend aloud. Touch the bend lightly. Is it warm? Stop when it breaks.
flow.parent: Typical: a plain steel clip often breaks after about 5 to 20 bends of 90 degrees, but clips differ a lot, so use the middle of your three. The bend feels warm. The break usually starts at the outside of the bend, where the metal is stretched most. Keep the clip low over a tray. Wear glasses if you have them.

check.q: A clip bends fine once, but snaps after 12 bends back and forth. What is the best explanation?
options: Each bend leaves a tiny change, and tiny cracks grow until it snaps
The clip got weaker because it was cold
The twelfth bend was bigger than the others
check.why: Every bend leaves a small change in the metal at the bend, and tiny cracks start and grow a little each time. After enough bends, the crack goes all the way through. This is fatigue. A bigger twelfth bend is not needed.

flow.context: In this step, you bend a clip back and forth by a big angle and count the bends to break.

flow.do: Bend three more clip wires back and forth by about 45 degrees, using the guide. Count the bends to break. Compare the middle count with the 90 degree clips. Write what you find.
flow.say: Now bend a clip by only half as far, about 45 degrees, three times. Count the bends until each breaks. Does it take more bends or fewer?
flow.kid: Bend clips by a smaller angle. Count the bends. More bends or fewer?
flow.think: Why might a smaller bend take more bends to break the clip?
flow.parent: A smaller bend usually takes many more bends, often three times as many or more, but the numbers vary a lot. If a clip does not break after 50 bends, stop and write 50 or more. This shows why engineers keep bends small in parts that flex many times.
flow.context: In this step, you bend a clip by a smaller angle and compare the number of bends to break.

activities.title: The Tape Measure Snap: why a thin strip folds suddenly

materials.item: a steel tape measure (not a cloth tailor's tape) with a curved tape, 3 metres, with a lock button. About Rs 50 to 100 at a hardware shop; borrow one if you can.
a strip of card about 3 centimetres wide and 30 centimetres long (cut from a cereal box), and a plastic ruler
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up holds the tape measure. The tape edge is sharp and can cut, and it can snap back fast. Keep your fingers away from the tape's edge, keep faces away from above the tape, and never let it spring back. Press the end gently.

schedule.what: Pull the tape out and see how stiff it is. Press the end until it kinks. Flatten the curve and try again. Measure how far a curved tape and a card strip stand out sideways.

activities.record: A drawing of the tape standing out, the tape kinked, and a note about what flattening the curve did. How far the curved tape, the card strip and the pinched tape stand out before they droop.
activities.context: In this activity, you pull out a tape measure and press the end until it suddenly folds. You find that a curved strip stays straight, then snaps into a fold.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a steel tape measure with 30 centimetres of tape sticking out straight.
setup.caption: 1. Pull out 30 centimetres of tape. It stands out straight.

setup.art: A finger gently pressing the end of the tape, with the tape suddenly kinking in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Press the end gently. It suddenly kinks.

setup.art: The tape squeezed flat between a finger and thumb, and bending easily.
setup.caption: 3. Flatten the curve with your fingers. Now the tape is floppy.

flow.do: A grown-up stands the tape measure on the table with the case flat. The grown-up pulls 30 centimetres of tape straight up and locks it. With one child, the parent holds and the child presses. With 2 to 4 children, one presses, one watches the middle, one writes.
flow.say: The tape is sticking out straight. If I press the end gently, what will happen? Will it bend slowly or suddenly?
flow.kid: The tape stands out straight. What happens when the end is pressed?

ask.q: What do you think will happen when you press the end?
good: It will bend slowly.
It will fold suddenly.
It will stay straight.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A curved tape stays surprisingly straight until the push reaches a limit, then folds all at once.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tape Measure Snap. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Press down gently on the end of the tape with one finger, along the line of the tape. Notice that nothing happens until a certain push, and then the tape kinks suddenly. Do it three times.
flow.say: Press gently down on the end. Watch the middle of the tape. Does it bend a little at a time, or all at once?
flow.kid: Press the end gently. Does the tape bend slowly or all at once?
flow.parent: Press gently along the tape, not sideways. Keep your fingers off the edge. The tape's curved cross-section makes it stiff, and it stays straight until the push passes a limit. Then it flips into a fold. This is buckling. A flat strip of card bends smoothly, with no sudden snap, and you can try it for comparison.

check.q: The tape stays straight as you press harder, and then folds suddenly. What does this tell you?
options: There is a limit to the push, and passing it makes the tape fold all at once
check.why: A buckling strip holds its shape until the push passes a limit. At the limit, a tiny extra push flips it into a bend. The push did not suddenly grow, and the tape is not broken. It springs back when released.

flow.context: In this step, you press the end of the tape and watch it fold suddenly.

flow.do: Squeeze the tape flat between your finger and thumb, and press the end again. Compare it with the first time. Now lay the case on the table edge and slowly pull the tape out sideways. Measure how far it stands out before it droops. Do the same with the card strip held at one end, and then pinch the tape flat just outside the case.
flow.say: Squeeze the tape flat for a moment. Now it is floppy. Why is the curved tape stiff, and the flat tape floppy?
flow.kid: Squeeze the tape flat. Is it still stiff? Try a flat card strip.
flow.think: Why does a curve make a thin strip stiff?
flow.parent: The curve makes the tape like a very shallow tube, and a tube resists bending much more than a flat strip of the same material. Engineers use curved and tubular shapes for the same reason, in bicycle frames, bamboo, drinking straws and aeroplane bodies. Typical: a curved tape stands out about half a metre to over a metre, depending on its width; a flat card strip droops at about 10 to 15 centimetres; a tape pinched flat folds at once. No tape measure? Roll a sheet of paper into a tube and tape it: stood on end, it holds a few books, while the same flat sheet folds at once.
flow.context: In this step, you flatten the tape and see how its curve made it stiff.

activities.title: The One-Second Bouncer: tune a bag to bounce once each second

materials.item: the rig from the Bounce Time test: the stick, two chairs, two linked rubber bands and the carrier bag

about 1.5 kilograms of rice in a few small bags, and a way to weigh out an exact load: a kitchen scale (borrow one, or ask a kirana to weigh for you), or a plastic bottle in the bag filled with water from a jug marked in millilitres (1 millilitre of water weighs about 1 gram; the empty bottle weighs about 20 grams)
a kitchen scale that shows grams, if you have one (water in a bottle can replace it)
a phone or clock that shows seconds, a calculator and a pencil
a soft cushion for the floor

activities.safety: Stand to the side and keep your face away from the bands. Never use more than 1 kilogram of load, and keep the cushion under the bag.

schedule.what: Time the bounce with 500 grams. Work out the load that gives one bounce each second. Test it. Adjust until ten bounces take about ten seconds.

activities.record: A table with each load, the time for ten bounces, the time for one bounce, and a note of whether it is too fast or too slow.
activities.context: In this activity, you use the rule you found in the Bounce Time test to choose the load that makes the bag bounce exactly once each second.

setup.art: A carrier bag on two linked rubber bands holding 500 grams of rice, and a stopwatch showing 7.5 seconds for ten bounces.
setup.caption: 1. Time ten bounces with 500 grams. Work out one bounce.

setup.art: A page with a calculation: the bounce time is 0.75 seconds, so the load needs to be 1.78 times as big, which is about 890 grams.
setup.caption: 2. Work out the load for a one-second bounce.

setup.art: A kitchen scale showing 890 grams with a bag of rice on it, and then the bag hanging on the bands with a stopwatch showing about 10 seconds.
setup.caption: 3. Weigh out that load, hang it and time ten bounces.

flow.do: Time ten bounces with 500 grams, three times. Find the middle time and divide by ten. Write the bounce time for one bounce. With one child, the parent times and the child counts and writes. With 2 to 4 children, one pulls, one times, one calculates the load, one writes. Swap after each try.
flow.say: Time ten bounces with half a kilogram, three times. Find the middle time. Divide by ten. That is the time of one bounce. Is it more or less than one second?
flow.kid: Time ten bounces with 500 g. Find one bounce. More or less than one second?
flow.parent: A bounce time under one second with 500 grams is usual. For example, 7.5 seconds for ten bounces is 0.75 seconds for one bounce. The task is to make it exactly one second.
flow.context: This is the first step of the One-Second Bouncer. You find the bounce time with a load of 500 grams.

flow.do: Work out the load needed. The bounce time must grow from your time to 1 second. Divide 1 by your time, and multiply the answer by itself. Multiply that by 500 grams. Write the load.
flow.say: We need a bigger bounce time, so we need a heavier load. Divide one second by your time. Multiply the answer by itself. That is how many times heavier. Multiply by 500 grams.
flow.kid: Divide 1 by your time. Multiply the answer by itself. Multiply by 500 g.
flow.think: Why do you multiply the answer by itself?
flow.parent: Bounce time grows with the square root of the load, so the load grows with the square of the time. For example, a bounce time of 0.75 seconds needs a time of 1 second. 1 divided by 0.75 is 1.33. 1.33 times 1.33 is 1.78. 1.78 times 500 grams is about 890 grams. Use your own numbers. If the answer is over 1000 grams, stop at 1000 grams, add a third band to the chain (that makes it softer and slower), and start again from the first step. If your time with 500 grams is already over one second, you need a lighter load.

check.q: A load of 500 g bounces in 0.5 seconds. About what load will bounce in 1 second?
check.why: To double the bounce time, the load must be four times as heavy, because the time grows with the square root of the load. Four times 500 grams is 2000 grams. The answer 1000 grams would only multiply the time by about 1.4. The answer 250 grams would shorten the time.

flow.context: In this step, you use the square-root rule to work out the load for a one-second bounce.

flow.do: Weigh out the new load on the kitchen scale. Hang it. Time ten bounces three times. Find the middle time. Write how close it is to ten seconds.
flow.say: Weigh out the load you worked out. Hang it and time ten bounces, three times. Is the middle time close to ten seconds?
flow.kid: Weigh the new load. Hang it. Time ten bounces. Is it near 10 seconds?
flow.parent: Rubber bands follow the rule only roughly, so you may land within about 10 percent of ten seconds. That is a good result for this activity. Timing by hand is only good to about 0.3 seconds, so a result of 9.5 to 10.5 is a fine place to stop.
flow.context: In this step, you test the load you worked out.

flow.do: If the time is too short, add a little rice. If it is too long, take a little out. Test again. Stop when ten bounces take between 9.5 and 10.5 seconds.
flow.say: Too fast, add some rice. Too slow, take some out. Try again. How close can you get to exactly one second a bounce?
flow.kid: Too fast? Add rice. Too slow? Take some out. Test again.

ask.q: How did your calculation compare with the real answer?
good: It was close but not exact, because rubber is not perfect.
I had to add a bit of rice.
The rule worked well.

flow.context: This is the last step of the One-Second Bouncer. You adjust the load to bring the time to one second.

projects.title: The Wobble Scale: weigh a lump of clay without gravity

materials.item: a plastic or thin wooden ruler about 30 centimetres long
a heavy book, masking tape and a table with a flat edge

modelling clay or plasticine, in 3 lumps of 20, 40 and 80 grams, and 2 mystery lumps between 30 and 70 grams (a small pack is about Rs 20 to 40). Keep the lumps in a polythene bag between the days. No kitchen scale? Ask a kirana, jeweller or medical shop to weigh the lumps; digital ones read to 1 gram.
a kitchen scale that shows grams, if you have one (or a shop that will weigh the lumps)
a phone or clock that shows seconds, squared paper and a pencil

projects.safety: A ruler can snap if it is bent too far, and plastic can crack into sharp edges. Flick it gently, keep your face away from it, and stop if it cracks. Clay is not food: wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Build the wobble scale. Time ten wobbles with three known lumps. Draw the graph.
Find the mass of two mystery lumps from their wobble times. Check each on the kitchen scale. Try the ruler on its side.

projects.record: A graph of the time for ten wobbles against the mass of the clay, and a table of two mystery lumps with the mass from your wobble scale and the mass from the kitchen scale.
projects.context: In this project, you build a scale from a ruler that finds the mass of clay by how fast it wobbles. Astronauts weigh themselves in a similar way in space.

setup.art: A ruler held under a heavy book on a table, with 20 centimetres sticking out over the edge and a lump of clay stuck to its end.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the ruler under a book. Stick a 20 gram lump of clay to its end.

setup.art: A finger gently flicking the end of the ruler down, and the clay wobbling up and down, with a stopwatch beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Flick the end down a little. Time ten wobbles.

setup.art: A graph with the mass of the clay along the bottom and the time for ten wobbles up the side, with three dots and a curve.
setup.caption: 3. Plot the times for 20, 40 and 80 grams. Draw a smooth curve.

setup.art: A mystery lump of clay on the ruler, a dotted line from its wobble time across to the curve and down to its mass.
setup.caption: 4. On day 2, time a mystery lump. Read its mass from the curve.

setup.art: The ruler under the book with 15, 20 and 25 centimetres sticking out in turn, and the same lump of clay on the end.
setup.caption: 5. Keep the same clay and change how much ruler sticks out. Time ten wobbles each time.

flow.do: Hold the ruler under a heavy book, with 20 centimetres sticking out over the table edge. Ask your child to guess what happens to the wobble when the clay is heavier, and why. Tape the ruler down over the book as well. Press the clay firmly round the end, with a strip of tape over it. With one child, the parent times and the child flicks and counts. With 2 to 4 children, one flicks, one times, one counts, one writes.
flow.say: A ruler is a springy stick. Put a lump of clay on its end and flick it. If the lump is heavier, will it wobble faster or slower? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stick clay on the ruler's end. Flick it. Will a heavier lump wobble faster or slower?

ask.q: Why do you think a heavier lump will change the wobble?
good: It is harder to move, so it wobbles slower.
The ruler pulls harder, so it wobbles faster.
A heavier lump pulls the end down more.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Press the book down hard, so that the ruler does not slip. If the ruler wobbles too fast to count with a 20 gram lump, slide more of it off the table, so that 25 centimetres stick out.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wobble Scale. You guess how the clay changes the wobble.

flow.do: Stick the 20 gram lump on the end of the ruler. Flick the end down about 1 centimetre and let go. Time ten wobbles. Do it three times and use the middle time. Do the same with 40 grams and 80 grams.
flow.say: Stick the lump to the end. Flick the end down a little and let go. Count ten wobbles and stop the clock. Do it three times. Then do the same with the 40 gram and 80 gram lumps.
flow.kid: Stick the clay on the end. Flick. Time ten wobbles. Do three times. Then try heavier clay.
flow.parent: Typical: about 3 to 8 seconds for ten wobbles with a thin, bendy plastic ruler. The 80 gram time should be about 1.7 to 2 times the 20 gram time, not exactly 2, because the ruler has a little mass of its own. A stiff or thick ruler wobbles faster: if ten wobbles take under 3 seconds, slide more of the ruler out, or time 20 wobbles and halve. If the ruler droops more than about 5 centimetres under the 80 gram lump, slide less out. Use the same flick size each time. If the wobbles die away before ten, count eight and divide.

check.q: Ten wobbles take 4 seconds with 20 grams. About how long do you expect for 80 grams?
check.why: 80 grams is 4 times 20 grams. The square root of 4 is 2, so the time doubles to about 8 seconds. The answer 16 seconds would multiply by 4. The answer 2 seconds would halve the time.

flow.context: In this step, you time the wobble with three known lumps of clay.

flow.do: Draw a graph with the mass in grams along the bottom and the time for ten wobbles up the side. Plot the three points. Draw a smooth curve through them, and carry it from 0 to 100 grams.
flow.say: Plot the three points. Draw a smooth curve through them. It will curve a little, because the time grows with the square root of the mass. This graph is your scale.
flow.kid: Plot three points. Draw a smooth curve through them.
flow.parent: The curve should bend over, rising quickly at first and then more slowly. Do not draw a straight line. Do not extend the curve far past 80 grams.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the graph that turns the wobble time into a mass.

flow.do: On day 2, stick a mystery lump on the ruler. Time ten wobbles three times. Find the time on your graph, go across to the curve, and then down to the mass. Do the same for the second lump. Weigh both on the kitchen scale and compare. With 2 or more children, each shapes a mystery lump in secret for another to weigh by wobble.
flow.say: Day two. Time ten wobbles of a mystery lump. Find the time up the side of the graph, go across to the curve and down to read the mass. Then check it on the kitchen scale.
flow.kid: Time a mystery lump. Use the graph to read its mass. Check it on the kitchen scale.

ask.q: How close was your wobble scale to the kitchen scale?
good: It was within a few grams.
It was close for one lump and not so close for the other.
It worked, which is surprising for a ruler.

flow.parent: A difference of 10 to 15 percent is a good result for a ruler. Use mystery lumps that weigh between 20 and 80 grams, so that the graph can be trusted. Lumps that are heavier or lighter than your known ones are out of range. Wobble times of the same lump can differ by a few tenths of a second, so use the middle of three.
flow.context: In this step, you find the mass of two mystery lumps with your wobble scale and check them.

flow.do: Keep the 40 gram lump on the end and change only how much ruler sticks out. Try 15, 20 and 25 centimetres. Time ten wobbles three times at each. Compare the three middle times.
flow.say: Now we change the ruler, not the clay. A short ruler is stiff and a long ruler is soft. Which will wobble faster? Time ten wobbles at 15, 20 and 25 centimetres with the 40 gram lump.
flow.kid: Change how much ruler sticks out: 15, 20 and 25 centimetres. Time ten wobbles with 40 g.
flow.think: The clay is pulled down by gravity, but does the wobble need gravity? What sets the beat?
flow.parent: The shorter ruler is stiffer and should wobble faster, and the longer one slower. Typical: 15 centimetres may take about half the time of 25 centimetres, but rulers differ. This is the idea behind the astronaut's mass scale. Weight needs gravity, but a wobble depends only on the mass and the stiffness. Gravity only bends the ruler down a little and then the wobble goes on around that place, so the same scale works in space.

check.q: With the same clay, a ruler sticking out 15 centimetres wobbles faster than the same ruler sticking out 25 centimetres. What does this show?
options: The beat depends on the stiffness as well as the mass
The clay is lighter on the short ruler
check.why: A short ruler is stiffer than a long one, and a stiffer spring gives a faster beat for the same mass. So the beat is set by the mass and the stiffness, and a wobble scale needs no gravity. The clay is the same on both, and a broken ruler would not wobble at all.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Wobble Scale. You change the stiffness of the ruler and see that the beat depends on it, not on gravity.

challenges.title: Soft Landing: keep a stack of coins standing
challenges.problem: Build a cushion inside a small box, so that a stack of coins standing inside stays standing when the box is dropped from 50 centimetres onto the floor. Find the tallest stack that you can protect.
constraints: The box must be a small cardboard box, about the size of a shoebox, and the cushion must fit inside it.
The coins must start in a neat stack on a small piece of card, standing upright, with nothing holding the stack except the cushion.
Drop the box flat from exactly 50 centimetres, measured from the bottom of the box.
Use only things from the house, such as rubber bands, paper cups, sponge, cloth, newspaper, cardboard and tape.
The score is the number of coins in the tallest stack that is still standing after the drop. Try each design three times.
materials: a small cardboard box with a lid, about the size of a shoebox
a pile of coins of the same size, at least 10
rubber bands, paper cups, a piece of sponge, cloth, newspaper and cardboard
a ruler, and a soft mat or folded blanket under the drop
challenges.safety: Drop the box over a soft mat or folded blanket. Keep your feet out of the way of the box. A grown-up cuts the cardboard if scissors are needed.
general: Pack the coins in a nest of crumpled newspaper, so that the paper squashes in the drop.
Put the card with the coin stack on a thick piece of sponge at the bottom of the box.
Fill the box with cloth around the card, so that the stack cannot slide.
creative: Hang the coin card in the middle of the box on rubber bands from all four sides, so that the stack floats and the bands soak up the jolt.
Stand the card on a tower of paper cups that crush gently in the drop.
Use a long band spring under the card and a sponge on top, to take both the bounce and the squash.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your design. Build it, and drop it three times. Change one thing and drop it three times again. Which design protects the tallest stack? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about springs and damping. You build a cushion that stops a jolt, so that a stack of coins stays standing.

setup.art: A page with three sketches of cushions: a box with crumpled newspaper, a card on a sponge, and a card hanging on rubber bands.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some ideas for the cushion.

setup.art: A box with the coin stack on a card inside a nest of rubber bands, held at 50 centimetres above a mat with a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Build the box. Hold it at 50 centimetres above the mat.

setup.art: The box on the mat after the drop, lid open, and a stack of coins still standing inside.
setup.caption: 3. Drop the box. Open the lid. Count how many coins stand.

flow.do: Read the problem and the constraints together. Ask your child to sketch two or three different cushions. Ask which design they think will work best, and why.
flow.say: We have to keep a stack of coins standing when the box is dropped. What could soak up the jolt? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Draw two or three cushion ideas. Which will work best? Why?

ask.q: What would stop a stack of coins from falling over when the box lands?
good: Something soft that squashes slowly.
Something springy that holds the stack in the middle.
Something that stops the stack sliding sideways.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Soft Landing challenge. You plan your cushion.

flow.do: Build your first cushion. Put a stack of 3 coins on the card. Close the box. Drop it flat from 50 centimetres onto the mat. Open the lid and see whether the stack is standing. Do it three times.
flow.say: Build your first design. Start with a stack of three coins. Drop the box from 50 centimetres and check. Do it three times. Write down how many times the stack stayed standing.
flow.kid: Build your cushion. Stack 3 coins. Drop the box. Is the stack standing?
flow.parent: Measure the drop height from the bottom of the box. Drop the box flat, without throwing it. If three coins stay standing every time, try five, then seven.

check.q: A box with a stiff metal spring under the card bounces the coins up and down and they fall over. A box with a soft sponge keeps them standing. What is the best explanation?
options: The sponge soaks up the movement as heat, while the stiff spring gives it back
check.why: A stiff spring stores the energy of the drop and gives it back as a bounce. The sponge squashes and loses the movement as a little heat, so there is less bounce. Weight is not the main reason.

flow.context: In this step, you build your first cushion and test it with a small stack.

flow.do: Change one thing at a time. You could change the thickness of the sponge, the number of bands or the height of the stack. Drop it again three times. Keep a table of designs and coins left standing.
flow.say: Change just one thing at a time. Did the stack do better or worse? What does that tell you about springs and soft things?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Drop three times. Did more coins stay standing?
flow.think: Does a springy cushion or a squashy cushion keep the stack standing better? Why?
flow.context: In this step, you improve your design and test one change at a time.

flow.do: Pick your best design. Write the tallest stack it protected. Say why you think it works in terms of springs, soft things and the jolt.
flow.say: Which design was best? How tall was the stack it protected? Why did it work?
flow.kid: Pick your best design. How tall was the stack? Why did it work?
flow.think: Why is a car seat springy and soft at the same time?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Soft Landing challenge. You pick your best design and explain why it works.

items.p: A band stretches 4 cm under a 2 N load. What is its stiffness?
items.why: Stiffness is the pull divided by the stretch. 2 divided by 4 is 0.5. The answer 8 multiplies the numbers instead of dividing them.

items.p: A bottle bounces on a band. If you pull it down twice as far before letting go, ten bounces take twice as long.
items.why: False. A bigger bounce goes further, but the band pulls harder and the bottle goes faster. The two effects cancel, so the time stays the same.

items.p: To find the time of one bounce, you time ten bounces and then ____ the time by ten.
items.why: Ten bounces take ten times as long as one, so you divide by ten. Timing ten shrinks the error of the stopwatch.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: the beat a spring and its load bounce at on their own
small pushes in time with the beat build a big movement
a material wearing out from being bent again and again
items.why: The natural beat is set by the load and the stiffness. Resonance needs pushes at that beat. Damping is where the movement goes as heat and sound. Fatigue is the slow cracking of a material that flexes over and over.

items.p: A bag of rice on a band bounces so that ten bounces take 6 seconds. You hang a bag that is four times heavier. About how long do ten bounces take?
items.why: Four times the load makes the bounce time twice as long, because the square root of 4 is 2. Twice 6 is 12. The answer 24 seconds multiplies by 4. The answer 6 seconds forgets that the load matters.

items.p: How does each change affect the bounce time of a load on a band?
items: two bands in a row instead of one
two bands side by side instead of one
taking the bag and bands to the Moon
items.why: A heavier load and a softer spring make the bounce slower. A stiffer spring makes it faster. The size of the bounce and the strength of gravity do not change the beat.

items.p: Why does a small push at the right moment make a swing go higher, when a bigger push at the wrong moment does not?
items.a: A swing has its own natural beat. A push at the right moment goes with the swing's movement and adds to it. Pushes at the right moment build up a big swing. A push at the wrong moment works against the movement or does not add, so the swing does not go higher.
items.why: A strong answer says that the swing has a natural beat, that a push in time adds to the movement, and that a push out of time does not.

items.p: One band stretches 10 cm under a packet. How far do two identical bands side by side stretch under the same packet?
items.why: Two bands side by side share the pull, so each carries half and stretches half as far. The pair is twice as stiff. The answer 20 cm is for two bands in a row.

items.p: Put these steps for timing a bounce fairly in order.
a: Pull the load down by a measured amount
Let go and start the clock
Count ten bounces and stop the clock
Take the middle time and divide it by ten
items.why: You set a fair start first, then time ten bounces, repeat to see the spread, and finally find the time of one bounce from the middle time.

items.p: A load bounces once every 0.8 seconds. How many bounces does it make in 20 seconds?
items.why: 20 divided by 0.8 is 25. A bounce time of 0.8 seconds means 1.25 bounces in every second, and 1.25 times 20 is 25.

items.p: A thick rubber band feels warm on your lip right after you stretch it quickly.
items.why: True. The long chains in the rubber line up as it stretches and give out a little heat. The change is small, so you need a quick stretch and a sensitive place like the lip.

items.p: Draw a graph with the pull along the bottom and the stretch up the side. Draw one line for a stiff spring and one for a soft spring. Label each line.
items.a: Two straight lines from the corner. The soft spring's line climbs steeply upward, since it stretches a lot for each newton. The stiff spring's line climbs gently, since it stretches only a little for each newton.
items.why: On a graph of stretch against pull, a soft spring has a steep line and a stiff spring has a gentle line. If the axes are the other way, the stiff one is steep.

items.p: What does a quartz watch count to keep time?
opts: The vibrations of a tiny crystal
items.why: A quartz watch uses a tiny crystal that vibrates 32,768 times each second. A chip counts the beats. A pendulum clock is a different kind of clock, and the Sun is used by a sundial.

items.p: Two bands in a row stretch 20 cm under a packet. How far will the same packet stretch two such bands side by side?
items.why: Two bands in a row stretch 20 cm, so each band alone stretches 10 cm. Two bands side by side stretch half as far as one, which is 5 cm.

items.p: A paper clip survives one big bend, but snaps after bending back and forth ten times. Explain what is happening.
items.a: Each bend leaves a tiny change in the metal at the bend. Tiny cracks start and grow a little with every bend. After enough bends, the crack goes right through and the clip snaps. This is called fatigue.
items.why: A strong answer names fatigue, and says that small changes add up with each bend until a crack goes through.

items.p: A bottle bounces on a band and the bounces get smaller and smaller. What stays about the same?
items.why: The size of the bounce falls, but the bounce time depends on the load and the stiffness, so it stays about the same. The speed of the bottle also falls, since smaller bounces are slower.

items.p: A load bounces in 0.4 seconds. A load 9 times heavier on the same spring bounces in about:
items.why: Nine times the load makes the bounce time three times as long, because the square root of 9 is 3. 3 times 0.4 is 1.2. The answer 3.6 multiplies by 9.

items.p: Four identical bands hang side by side holding one load. How does the stiffness of the group compare with one band?
items.why: Bands side by side share the pull and their stiffnesses add. Four bands are four times as stiff. A quarter as stiff would be for four bands in a row.

items.p: A spring stretches 2 cm under 6 N. Its stiffness is ____ N for each cm.
items.why: 6 divided by 2 is 3. The spring needs 3 newtons for each centimetre.

items.p: A bottle on a band would bounce more slowly on the Moon than on Earth, since gravity is weaker there.
items.why: False. The bounce time depends on the load and the stiffness, and gravity does not come into it. The bottle would bounce at the same beat on the Moon.

items.p: Is each of these an example of resonance?
items: pushing a swing at the end of each swing
a radio picking out one station
a ball bouncing lower and lower on the floor
one tuning fork making a second fork ring
a paper clip snapping after many bends
pushing a swing at random moments
items.why: Resonance is when pushes or signals at a thing's own natural beat build up a big response. A ball getting lower is damping, and a snapped paper clip is fatigue.

items.p: A load of 1 kg bounces in 1 second. What load on the same spring would bounce in 3 seconds, in kilograms?
items.why: To triple the bounce time, the load must be 3 times 3, which is 9 times as heavy. So the load is 9 kilograms.

items.p: Match each clock or scale to the springy thing it uses.
items.why: Each one counts or times a springy beat. The watch counts the swings of a balance spring, the quartz watch counts a crystal, the atomic clock counts atoms, and a spring seat times the bounce to find a mass.

items.p: Why does a rubber band feel warm after a quick stretch?
opts: The long chains line up as they stretch and give out a little heat
The band is rubbing against the air
The band was warm inside before
items.why: When rubber is stretched, the tangled chains line up, which gives out some heat. This is different from friction with the air, and it happens even in a clean, cool band.

items.p: Soldiers are told to break step when they cross a bridge. Explain why, using the idea of a natural beat.
items.a: A bridge can have a natural beat, like a swing. If many people march in time, their steps might push at the bridge's natural beat. Each step would add to the last, and the bridge could sway more and more. Breaking step means the pushes are not all in time.
items.why: A strong answer says that a bridge can have a natural beat, and that regular pushes at that beat could build up a large movement.

items.p: Two children talk about the Tacoma Narrows Bridge, which fell in 1940.

views.who: Dev, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The wind pushed at the bridge's natural beat, so the swing built up. That is resonance.

views.who: Asha, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The wind was steady, not beating at the bridge's beat. The bridge's own twisting took energy from the wind, which is a different effect.

items.ask: Whose explanation fits what engineers found later? What kind of evidence would decide?
items.a: Answers vary. Engineers who studied the bridge later found that the wind was steady and the bridge's own movement drew energy from it, an effect called flutter. This supports Asha's view. Evidence from wind tunnel tests on models decided it.
items.why: A good answer says that Asha's explanation fits the later studies, and says what kind of test, such as a model in a wind tunnel, could decide.

items.p: Twenty bounces of a bag take 15 seconds. How long does one bounce take, in seconds?
items.why: 15 divided by 20 is 0.75. Timing twenty bounces and dividing gives a more exact answer than timing one.

items.p: A pendulum clock runs down, and its swings get smaller. What happens to the time for one swing?
items.why: For small swings, the time of one swing does not depend on how big the swing is. This is why pendulum clocks can keep time even as the swings get smaller.

items.p: Put these in order to show how small pushes build a big swing.
a: Pull the swing back and let go
Push gently as it moves away
Wait for it to come back
Push gently again at the same moment
Each push adds to the swing, and it grows high
items.why: The pushes must come at the same moment in each swing. Each one adds to the movement, so the swing builds up.

items.p: Draw two bands in a row and two bands side by side, each holding the same packet. If one band stretches 10 cm, write how far each group stretches.
items.a: Two bands in a row, hanging in a chain with the packet at the bottom, labelled 20 cm. Two bands side by side, both holding the packet, labelled 5 cm.
items.why: Two in a row add their stretches, so 20 cm. Two side by side share the pull, so each stretches 5 cm.

items.p: A stiffer spring is always a stronger spring.
items.why: False. Stiff means a big pull for a small stretch. Strong means able to take a big load without breaking. A stiff glass rod breaks easily, and a soft steel spring can take a very big load.

items.p: Why can a spring seat find an astronaut's mass in space, when a bathroom scale cannot?
opts: The bounce time depends on the mass and the stiffness, and not on gravity
The bathroom scale is too heavy
items.why: A bathroom scale measures how hard you press on it, which needs gravity. A spring seat bounces at a beat set by the mass and the stiffness, so it works wherever you are.

items.p: Using the idea of the pull of the spring, explain why a big bounce takes the same time as a small bounce.
items.a: A bigger bounce means the spring is stretched further, so it pulls harder. A harder pull speeds the load up more. The load goes further but also faster, and the two effects cancel, so the time stays the same.
items.why: A strong answer says that the pull grows with the stretch, that the load is speeded up more, and that the longer path is covered at a higher speed.

items.p: A spring bounces in 2 seconds with a 1 kg load. What load would make it bounce in 1 second?
items.why: To halve the bounce time, the load must be 4 times lighter, because the square root of 4 is 2. A quarter of 1 kg is 0.25 kg. The answer 0.5 kg would only shorten the time by about 30 percent.

items.p: Two identical springs, each with a stiffness of 0.5 N for each cm, are placed side by side. What is the stiffness of the pair, in newtons for each centimetre?
items.why: Side by side, stiffnesses add. 0.5 plus 0.5 is 1 newton for each centimetre.

items.p: A singer can break a wine glass with a loud note. Explain what the note must match, and why a louder note at the wrong pitch does not break it.
items.a: A wine glass has a natural beat, which is the pitch it rings at when tapped. If the singer's note matches that beat, each push of sound adds to the glass's vibration, until it shakes so much that it breaks. A louder note at the wrong pitch is out of time with the glass, so the pushes do not add up.
items.why: A strong answer says that the note must match the glass's natural beat, so the pushes add up, and that a push out of time does not build up.

items.p: A quartz watch crystal vibrates 32,768 times each second. A chip halves the count 15 times to get one tick each second. Why 15 times?
opts: Because 15 is the number of seconds in a quarter minute
items.why: Halving 32,768 fifteen times gives 1, because 2 multiplied by itself 15 times is 32,768. The other reasons are made up.

items.p: A metal part that is bent only a little each time cannot ever break from bending.
items.why: False. Even small bends, repeated many times, can start and grow cracks. This is fatigue, and it is why engineers inspect parts that flex over and over.

items.p: Does each change alter the bounce time of a load on a spring?
items: pulling the load further down before letting go
taking the experiment to the Moon
joining two springs in a row
starting with a harder flick but the same load
items.why: The bounce time is set by the load and the stiffness. The size of the start and the strength of gravity do not change it.

items.p: Two friends argue about string theory, the idea that particles are tiny vibrating strings.

views.who: Ravi, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A theory must be testable. Until string theory can be tested, it is not science.

views.who: Meena, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: It is too early to judge. The mathematics is a guide, and tests may be found later.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with, and why? What would count as a test?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says what a test would need to do, such as predicting something that can be measured and that other theories do not predict, and gives a reason for the view.
items.why: Both views have a point. Science needs tests in the end, and new ideas are often explored before the tests are known. A good answer says what a test might look like.

items.p: A bounce time of 0.5 seconds means a frequency of ____ hertz.
items.why: The frequency is the number of cycles in one second. One cycle takes 0.5 seconds, so two cycles fit in one second, which is 2 hertz.

items.p: Why do aeroplane windows have round corners rather than square ones?
opts: Cracks from fatigue start easily at sharp corners
items.why: Sharp corners concentrate the stress, so fatigue cracks start there. After two Comet airliners broke up in 1954, round corners became the rule. Lightness and looks were not the reason.

items.p: The surface of the Sun rises and falls once about every 5 minutes. About how many times does it do this in 2 hours?
items.why: Two hours is 120 minutes. 120 divided by 5 is 24.

items.p: You have two unlabelled springs and want to know which is stiffer. Describe two different ways to find out, using a load, a ruler and a clock.
items.a: Method 1: hang the same load on each spring and measure the stretch. The one that stretches less is stiffer. Method 2: hang the same load on each, make it bounce and time ten bounces. The one with the shorter time is stiffer.
items.why: A strong answer gives a fair test for each method, with the same load, and says which result means stiffer.

items.p: Draw a graph showing how big the bag's bounce is, as the speed of the shaking hand goes from slow to fast. Mark where the bag's natural beat is.
items.a: A hill-shaped curve: low for slow shaking, rising to a peak at the natural beat, and falling again for fast shaking. The peak is marked as the natural beat.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a peak at the natural beat, and small bounces for hand speeds that are much slower or faster.

items.p: A pendulum and a spring with a load both keep good time on Earth. Which one would keep the same time on the Moon?
opts: Both would keep the same time
items.why: A spring's beat depends on the load and the stiffness, and not on gravity. A pendulum depends on gravity, which is weaker on the Moon, so it would swing more slowly.

items.p: Put these steps for choosing a load that gives a bounce time you want in order.
a: Time ten bounces with a known load
Divide by ten to get one bounce
Find how many times longer you want the bounce to be
Multiply the known load by the answer
items.why: The load grows with the square of the time you want. So you find the factor for the time, multiply it by itself, and use it on the load.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? A balance spring, a quartz crystal, a caesium atom, a sundial.
items.a: The sundial, because it tells the time from the shadow of the Sun. The other three keep time by vibrating.
items.why: A balance spring, a quartz crystal and a caesium atom all vibrate at a steady beat that a clock counts. A sundial has nothing that vibrates.

quiz.p: What does the stiffness of a spring tell you?
opts: How much pull it needs for each centimetre it stretches
quiz.why: Stiffness is the pull divided by the stretch. A stiff spring needs a big pull for a small stretch.

quiz.p: Why are two identical bands side by side stiffer than one band?
opts: They share the pull, so each one stretches less
quiz.why: Each band carries half the pull and stretches half as far, so the pair is twice as stiff. Length and weight are not the reason.

quiz.p: Why do we time ten bounces and divide, rather than time one bounce?
opts: A stopwatch cannot time a fraction of a second well, and dividing shrinks the error
One bounce is not a real bounce
quiz.why: A small timing error of a quarter of a second is a big part of one bounce, but a small part of ten bounces. Dividing by ten shares the error out.

quiz.p: A bottle on a band is pulled down 3 cm and let go. Later it is pulled down 6 cm and let go. What can you say about the bounce time?
opts: The 6 cm bounce takes twice as long
The 6 cm bounce takes half as long
quiz.why: The band pulls harder when stretched further, so the bottle goes faster. The bounce time stays about the same.

quiz.p: A load bounces in 2 seconds. A load 4 times heavier, on the same spring, will bounce in about:
quiz.why: Four times the load doubles the bounce time, because the square root of 4 is 2. Twice 2 seconds is 4 seconds.

quiz.p: A spring is swapped for one that is 4 times stiffer, with the same load. What happens to the bounce time?
quiz.why: A stiffer spring pulls harder and speeds the load up faster. Four times the stiffness halves the bounce time.

opts: Pushes in time with a thing's natural beat building a big movement
quiz.why: Resonance happens when pushes come at the natural beat of a springy thing, and each push adds to the last one. It is about timing, not loudness.

quiz.p: A parent wants to push a child's swing so it goes as high as possible. When should each push come?
opts: As the swing is starting to move away, in the same direction
While the swing is coming towards the parent
quiz.why: A push in the direction of the swing's movement adds to it. A push against the movement, or at random, does not build up the swing.

quiz.p: What happens to the temperature of a rubber band that is stretched quickly and then let go?
opts: It warms up when stretched and cools when let go
It cools when stretched and warms when let go
quiz.why: The rubber chains line up when stretched, which gives out heat. When let go, they tangle again and take in heat from around, so the band cools.

quiz.p: What is fatigue in a material?
opts: Cracks growing from being bent or stretched again and again
A material getting tired when it is warm
A material that is too heavy
quiz.why: Fatigue is the slow growth of tiny cracks in a material that flexes many times, even if each flex is small. It ends in a sudden break.

quiz.p: Which of these keeps time by the swing of a fine coiled spring?
quiz.why: A mechanical watch has a balance spring that swings a small wheel at a steady beat. A sundial uses the Sun's shadow, and a candle clock uses burning.

quiz.p: What is used to define the length of one second today?
quiz.why: Since 1967, a second has been defined as exactly 9,192,631,770 vibrations of a caesium atom. These vibrations are far steadier than a pendulum or a heartbeat.

open_questions.q: Are the smallest particles tiny vibrating strings?
open_questions.why_open: String theory is mathematically rich, but nobody has found an experiment that can test it. Some physicists think it is the most promising idea, and others doubt it.

open_questions.q: How does a Venus flytrap count touches, and where does she keep the memory?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know the trap needs two touches within about twenty seconds. They are still working out the chemistry and the electrical signals that store the first touch.

open_questions.q: Can we predict exactly when a metal part will fail from fatigue?
open_questions.why_open: Engineers can estimate the number of bends a part will take, but the exact moment depends on tiny flaws that are hard to see. They use safety margins and inspections.

open_questions.q: Why does the Sun oscillate in the way it does, and what does it tell us about its inside?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists learn a great deal from the Sun's ringing. They are still working out a few puzzles about the Sun's centre and its magnetic field.

open_questions.q: How steady can a clock be?
open_questions.why_open: Atomic clocks keep getting steadier, and new kinds are being built. Nobody knows how far this can go, or whether there is a limit.

open_questions.q: Why do the same simple rules of springs and beats appear in swings, atoms and stars?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists can explain how this works with mathematics. Why nature repeats the same patterns at such different sizes is a question people are still asking.

maths.problem: Look at the table of three made-up springs, all pulled with 2 N. They stretched 6 cm, 2 cm and 1 cm. Which spring is the stiffest? How many times stiffer than the 6 cm spring is the 1 cm spring?
maths.answer: The 1 cm spring is the stiffest. It is 6 times as stiff as the 6 cm spring.
maths.explain: The stiffnesses are 2 divided by 6, which is about 0.33, 2 divided by 2, which is 1, and 2 divided by 1, which is 2. 2 divided by 0.33 is about 6. You can also see it directly: the same pull stretches the first spring 6 times as far as the third.
maths.context: In the Stiffness League, you hang the same load on stretchy things and compare how far each stretches.
maths.why_maths: Comparing stiffness as a ratio tells you how many times stiffer one spring is than another, which a plain subtraction does not show.

maths.problem: In the Bounce Time test, ten bounces took 8.4 seconds. How long does one bounce take? How many bounces happen in one second, to one decimal place?
maths.answer: One bounce takes 0.84 seconds. About 1.2 bounces happen in each second.
maths.explain: 8.4 divided by 10 is 0.84. One divided by 0.84 is about 1.19, which rounds to 1.2. A bounce time of 0.84 seconds is a frequency of about 1.2 hertz.
maths.context: In the Bounce Time test, you time ten bounces of a bag of rice on two rubber bands.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the time for ten bounces by ten shares out the timing error, and the frequency tells you how fast the beat is.

maths.problem: A 250 gram load bounces ten times in 5 seconds. Use the square-root rule to predict the time for ten bounces with 1000 grams, and with 2250 grams.
maths.answer: 10 seconds with 1000 grams, and 15 seconds with 2250 grams.
maths.explain: 1000 grams is 4 times 250 grams, and the square root of 4 is 2, so 2 times 5 is 10 seconds. 2250 grams is 9 times 250 grams, and the square root of 9 is 3, so 3 times 5 is 15 seconds.
maths.context: In the Bounce Time test, you found that four times the load makes the bounce time about twice as long.
maths.why_maths: The square-root rule lets you predict a bounce time before you test it. Perfect squares like 4 and 9 make the predictions easy to check.

maths.problem: A band has a stiffness of 0.5 N for each cm. A 6 N packet hangs on it. How far does it stretch? How far do two such bands stretch in a row, and how far side by side?
maths.answer: 12 cm for one band, 24 cm for two in a row, and 6 cm for two side by side.
maths.explain: 6 divided by 0.5 is 12 cm for one band. Two in a row are half as stiff, with 0.25, and 6 divided by 0.25 is 24 cm. Two side by side are twice as stiff, with 1, and 6 divided by 1 is 6 cm.
maths.context: You have learnt that bands in a row are softer, and bands side by side are stiffer.
maths.why_maths: Working out the stiffness of a group first, and then dividing the pull by it, shows how joining springs changes the stretch.

maths.problem: Look at the line graph of made-up results from the Favourite Beat test. At which hand speed did the bag bounce the most? How many times bigger was that bounce than the bounce at 30 beats a minute?
maths.answer: The biggest bounce was at 80 beats a minute. It was 9 times bigger than at 30 beats a minute.
maths.explain: The tallest point is at 80 beats a minute, with a bounce of 9 cm. At 30 beats a minute, the bounce was 1 cm. 9 divided by 1 is 9. The peak is at the bag's natural beat.
maths.context: In the Favourite Beat test, you shake the top of the bands at different speeds and measure how big the bag's bounce gets. The graph shows made-up results.

chart.title: Size of the bag's bounce for each hand speed (made-up numbers)

maths.why_maths: A line graph shows where a pattern peaks. The peak tells you the natural beat, and a ratio tells you how much the right beat helps.

maths.problem: A metronome ticks 80 times each minute. How many seconds are there between ticks? The bag's natural bounce time is 0.8 seconds. Is the metronome a little faster or a little slower than the bag?
maths.answer: 0.75 seconds between ticks. The metronome is a little faster than the bag.
maths.explain: 60 seconds divided by 80 ticks is 0.75 seconds. The bag takes 0.8 seconds for one bounce. 0.75 is shorter than 0.8, so the metronome is a little faster.
maths.context: In the Favourite Beat test, you use a metronome or a count to move your hand at a steady speed.
maths.why_maths: Turning beats each minute into seconds for one beat lets you compare the hand's speed with the bag's bounce time.

maths.problem: A quartz watch crystal vibrates 32,768 times each second. A chip halves the count again and again until it gets 1. How many times does it halve?
maths.explain: 32,768 halves to 16,384, then 8,192, then 4,096, then 2,048, then 1,024, then 512, then 256, then 128, then 64, then 32, then 16, then 8, then 4, then 2, then 1. That is 15 halvings. It is because 2 multiplied by itself 15 times is 32,768.
maths.context: You have learnt that quartz watches count the vibrations of a tiny crystal and turn them into ticks.
maths.why_maths: Halving over and over is the same as dividing by powers of 2. This is how a fast beat is slowed down to a tick you can see.

maths.problem: The Sun's surface rises and falls once about every 5 minutes. About how many times does that happen in an hour, and in a day?
maths.answer: About 12 times in an hour and about 288 times in a day.
maths.explain: An hour has 60 minutes, and 60 divided by 5 is 12. A day has 24 hours, and 24 times 12 is 288.
maths.context: You have learnt that the Sun rings like a bell, with its surface rising and falling every few minutes.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a small number of beats by many hours shows how many cycles a long-running oscillation makes.

how_we_found_out.story: For centuries, sailors could find how far north or south they were, but not how far east or west. To find that, they needed to know the exact time at a faraway port, and compare it with the Sun's time on their ship. Pendulum clocks failed at sea, because the rocking of the waves threw off the swing. In 1714, the British Parliament asked experts, including Isaac Newton, how to solve the problem. Newton told them that a clock accurate enough for use at sea had not yet been made. Many astronomers believed that the answer would come from the Moon and the stars. John Harrison, an English clockmaker, thought otherwise. He built clocks and watches with springs and balanced wheels in place of pendulums, so that rocking could not stop them. His fourth, a large watch finished in 1759, was tested on a voyage to Jamaica in 1761. It was found to be only about five seconds slow after the voyage. A balance spring keeps its beat however the ship tilts.
how_we_found_out.who: John Harrison (1693 to 1776), an English clockmaker
how_we_found_out.when: He finished his fourth sea timekeeper in 1759, and it was tested at sea in 1761 and 1762
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many experts believed that no clock could keep accurate time on a rocking ship, with changes in heat, damp and gravity. Harrison showed it could be done, with a clock that used a spring, not a pendulum, and the sea trial proved it.

roots.context: We have bounced bags, shaken bands at the right beat and watched a clip tire out. Now we ask what the beat of a spring tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Favourite Beat test, small hand movements made the bag bounce high when they matched its own beat. At other beats, the same movements made it bounce hardly at all. A push adds to the last push only if it comes at the right moment. So what a push does depends on its timing as well as its strength.
deep_truth.habit: We think the result of a push depends on how hard it is. That leaves out timing, which can make a tiny push build into a huge movement.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Favourite Beat test, a hand movement of about 2 centimetres made the bag bounce much further at its own beat than at other beats. If your own numbers differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: Your arm swings like a pendulum when you walk. Each person has an easy walking pace, and it is the pace that takes the least effort.
three.what_is_life: Many living beings keep a steady beat. A hummingbird's wings, a cricket's chirp and a human heart each repeat at a rhythm that suits the body.
three.what_is_this_world: A bond between two atoms, a swing, a bridge and the surface of the Sun all have a natural beat. The world is full of springy things, each with its own favourite rhythm.

roots.thread: A swing, a band, a watch, a bond between two atoms and the whole Sun all behave as springs with a natural beat. They are very different things, and one rule describes all of them. Atoms hold on to each other with the electric force, and that pull-back is what makes anything springy. Whether there is a still deeper layer, such as tiny vibrating strings, is an idea that nobody has yet been able to test.

teachings.teaching: To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven.
teachings.link: A push builds a swing only at the right moment. The same push at another moment adds nothing.
A parent who pushes a swing well does not push harder. She pushes at the right moment, and the swing does the rest.

science.text: Every springy thing has a natural beat set by its stiffness and its load, and pushes at that beat build a large movement. This is resonance.
Whether the smallest particles are tiny vibrating strings is an idea that has not been tested.

other_view.view: Resonance is simple mathematics that holds for anything that can be described by a spring and a mass. Talk of a world full of favourite beats adds nothing to the equations.

practice.title: Find your own easy beat
practice.say: Stand up and let one arm hang loose. Swing it forwards and backwards gently, without pushing hard. Notice how it settles into a steady beat. Now try to swing it faster, and then slower. Feel how much harder that is. Go back to the easy beat and breathe in slowly three times.
practice.kid: Let one arm hang loose. Swing it gently. Find the easy beat. Breathe in slowly three times.

ask: Is the strength of a push the only thing that decides what it does?
Your arm has an easy beat that takes the least effort. Does every part of you have one?
If a bond between two atoms, a swing and the Sun all have a natural beat, is having a beat a fact about the thing, or about how we describe it?

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Bounce Time and Favourite Beat tests use two wide rubber bands linked like a chain, hung from a stick on two heavy chairs. Bands differ a lot. If the bands look thin and pale with 1 kilogram, add a third band to the chain and use it for every test, and never go above 1 kilogram. Rubber bands damp a bounce quickly, so ten bounces is the most to count, and eight is fine. Expect about 7 to 11 seconds for ten bounces with 500 grams. The ratio of the 1000 gram time to the 250 gram time is often a little under 2, because rubber stiffens when stretched, and 1.5 to 2.1 is a good result. In the Favourite Beat test, the best hand speed is a range rather than a single value, because rubber damps the response. A metronome app helps, and counting seconds aloud against a clock also works. The Stiffness League needs the spring from a retractable pen, which a grown-up must take out. The Tired Clip and the Tape Measure Snap need a grown-up, because clip ends and tape edges are sharp. The Wobble Scale needs a ruler that wobbles slowly enough to count, so slide more of it off the table if it wobbles too fast. In Soft Landing, three coins is an easy start. Facts to check before use: the details of John Harrison's sea trial, Sophie Germain's prize attempts, the number of touches and time window of the flytrap, and the Skylab mass device.
